dengue.name: Dengue
dengue.source: World Health Organization — Dengue and severe dengue fact sheet
key_facts: Dengue is a viral infection spread by infected mosquitoes.
Roughly half the world's population is currently at risk, with an estimated 100–400 million infections occurring each year.
It is most common in tropical and sub-tropical urban and semi-urban areas.
Most infections are mild or symptom-free, but a smaller share of cases become severe and can be fatal.
There is no specific antiviral treatment; prevention relies mainly on controlling mosquito populations and avoiding bites.
About 1 in 4 people infected with dengue will actually get sick from it.
Of those who do get sick, about 1 in 20 will go on to develop severe dengue.
dengue.overview: Dengue, sometimes called break-bone fever, is spread from mosquitoes to people and is more common in warm, tropical climates than in temperate ones. Most infected people have no symptoms at all and recover without ever knowing they were infected. Among those who do develop symptoms, most recover within one to two weeks, though a minority progress to severe dengue and require hospital care.
dengue.transmission: The virus is carried mainly by the Aedes aegypti mosquito. After biting an infected person, the virus takes roughly 8–12 days to replicate inside the mosquito before it can be passed on to someone else. An infected person can pass the virus to mosquitoes for about 4–5 days on average. Two related mosquito species carry the virus -- Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus -- and both can bite during the day as well as at night, and both live and lay eggs in and around homes (in containers that collect water, such as buckets, flowerpots, and discarded containers). A woman infected with dengue during pregnancy can also pass the virus to her fetus, which can contribute to low birth weight, premature birth, or fetal loss. Much more rarely, dengue has also been transmitted through blood transfusions, organ transplants, or needlestick injuries, and there is some evidence it may occasionally spread through sexual contact; the virus has been detected in breast milk as well, though transmission through breastfeeding has not been confirmed, and mothers are still encouraged to breastfeed given how low that risk appears to be.
dengue.symptom_onset: When symptoms occur, they usually begin 4–10 days after infection and last 2–7 days. A second dengue infection carries a higher risk of progressing to severe dengue.
dengue.escalation_note: These warning signs often appear after the fever has already gone down, and mean the person should seek medical care immediately.
prevention: Wear clothing that covers as much skin as possible
Use insecticide-treated mosquito nets, especially if sleeping during the day
Install window and door screens
Use mosquito repellents containing DEET, Picaridin, or IR3535
Use mosquito coils or vaporizers
Empty, clean, or cover water-storage containers weekly to stop mosquito breeding
Dispose of solid waste and remove containers that can collect standing water
When travelling to a dengue-risk area: review destination-specific travel health advisories beforehand and visit a travel clinic for pre-trip advice
Pack an EPA-registered insect repellent and a supply of paracetamol/acetaminophen for the trip
During the stay, prefer air-conditioned or well-screened accommodation, and use a bed net if that isn't available

After returning, keep preventing mosquito bites for about 3 weeks (even without symptoms) and watch for symptoms for about 2 weeks, since a still-infected traveller can pass the virus on to local mosquitoes
dengue.treatment: There is no specific medicine for dengue. Paracetamol (acetaminophen) can be used for pain and fever, but NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and aspirin should be avoided since they increase bleeding risk. Rest and adequate fluid intake are important, and hospitalization is often required for severe cases. For mild cases, care can usually happen at home: rest as much as possible, drink plenty of fluids (water or drinks with added electrolytes), and take paracetamol/acetaminophen for fever and pain -- never aspirin or ibuprofen. Anyone caring for someone with dengue at home should also help prevent further mosquito bites during the first week of illness, since the virus is present in the blood during this window and a mosquito that bites an infected person can go on to infect others.
dengue.testing: A blood test is the only way to confirm a dengue diagnosis. Laboratory confirmation isn't required to manage the illness, though -- a healthcare provider may treat based on symptoms alone. Providers may also test for similar viruses such as Zika or chikungunya, since these cause overlapping symptoms and are spread by the same mosquitoes.
dengue.vaccine_notes: Vaccine availability is limited and evolving. Dengvaxia was approved in 2021 for children aged 9-16 with a lab-confirmed prior dengue infection living in high-transmission areas, but its manufacturer discontinued production in 2024 due to low global demand, and no dengue vaccine is currently available in the United States. Separately, a newer vaccine, Qdenga, is licensed in some other countries, generally for ages 6-16 in high-transmission settings. Because coverage varies so much by country and age group, vaccination should never be assumed -- avoiding mosquito bites remains the primary protection for almost everyone.

dengue.infant_care: Dengue symptoms in infants can be hard to recognize since they resemble other common childhood infections, and there is no specific medicine for dengue at any age. At-home care focuses on controlling fever, giving plenty of fluids, and watching closely for warning signs. Contact the child's pediatrician immediately if the infant shows few or no tears when crying, or a sunken soft spot on the head or eyes. Signs of more severe dehydration -- ongoing sleepiness or unusual fussiness, sunken eyes, cool or discolored hands or feet, or urinating only 1-2 times a day -- mean the child should be taken to an urgent care clinic or emergency room right away. To protect other family members, keep preventing mosquito bites around a sick infant, especially during the first week of illness, since the virus is present in the blood during this window and a mosquito that bites the infant could go on to infect others.
dengue.areas_at_risk: Almost half the world's population -- an estimated 4 billion people -- live in areas with some risk of dengue, and anyone who lives in or travels to such an area is potentially at risk of infection. Risk is present across much of the Americas, Africa, the Middle East, Asia, and the Pacific Islands, including many popular tourist destinations. India is classified as a frequent/continuous risk country, meaning it has a sustained pattern of locally-acquired dengue cases. The mosquitoes that spread dengue mainly live at lower altitudes (roughly below 6,500 feet), so the chances of infection drop sharply at higher elevations. Travelers should check destination-specific advisories before a trip, since risk can vary significantly even within the same country or region.

malaria.name: Malaria
malaria.source: World Health Organization — Malaria fact sheet
key_facts: Malaria is a life-threatening but preventable and curable disease spread by mosquito bites.
It is caused by a parasite and does not spread directly from person to person.
Globally there were an estimated 282 million cases and 610,000 deaths in 2024, across 80 countries.
The WHO African Region carries a disproportionate share of the global burden — about 95% of both cases and deaths.
Children under 5 account for roughly three-quarters of malaria deaths in that region.
malaria.overview: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted through the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Five parasite species infect humans; P. falciparum is the deadliest and most common in Africa, while P. vivax dominates in most other regions. Left untreated, P. falciparum malaria can progress to severe illness and death within 24 hours, which is why prompt testing and treatment matter.
malaria.symptom_onset: Early symptoms usually start 10–15 days after an infective mosquito bite and can be mild, especially in people who've had malaria before — which is why testing early, rather than assuming it's a normal fever, is important.
high_risk_groups: Infants and young children with little or no prior exposure to malaria
Travelers coming from areas with no malaria (little to no built-up exposure)
People heavily exposed to bites from mosquitoes carrying P. falciparum
People living in rural areas with limited access to healthcare
malaria.escalation_note: Anyone showing severe symptoms should get emergency medical care immediately; early treatment of mild malaria can prevent it from progressing to severe disease.
prevention: Sleep under insecticide-treated mosquito nets
Use repellents containing DEET, IR3535, or icaridin after dusk
Use mosquito coils or vaporizers
Wear protective clothing
Use window screens
Travelers should consult a doctor about preventive medication (chemoprophylaxis) before visiting malaria-endemic areas
malaria.treatment: Malaria always requires medical treatment and should never be self-treated. Diagnosis is confirmed with a microscopy test or rapid diagnostic test. Artemisinin-based combination therapies are the most effective treatment for P. falciparum; chloroquine is used for sensitive P. vivax infections, sometimes with primaquine added to prevent relapse. Treatment choice and duration also depend on the likely geographic source of the infection (since drug resistance patterns vary by region), the patient's age, and whether they are pregnant or breastfeeding, alongside how severe the illness already is by the time treatment starts -- which is why starting treatment as early as possible matters so much. Patients are often hospitalized during malaria treatment, particularly for more severe cases.
malaria.transmission: Malaria spreads when an infective Anopheles mosquito bites a person. Only female Anopheles mosquitoes transmit malaria between people: the mosquito must first bite someone already infected to pick up the parasite, and roughly a week later it can pass the parasite on to the next person it bites. Malaria is not contagious in the way a cold or flu is -- it cannot spread through casual contact, close physical contact, or sexual contact. Very rarely, it can also spread through blood transfusions, organ transplants, sharing needles or syringes contaminated with infected blood, or from a mother to her unborn child before or during delivery.
malaria.incubation_period: The time between an infective mosquito bite and the first symptoms -- called the incubation period -- is typically 7 to 30 days, though this varies by the specific parasite species involved, and some people don't feel ill until anywhere from about a week up to a year or more after infection. Some malaria parasite species can also lie dormant in the liver for months or years after the initial infection before re-emerging to infect red blood cells and cause another episode of illness; proper diagnosis and treatment can prevent illness from these dormant parasites.
malaria.testing: Only a healthcare provider can diagnose malaria, and only a lab test using a small blood sample can confirm it -- anyone who has traveled in the past year to an area where malaria spreads should get tested as soon as symptoms appear, since delayed diagnosis is a leading cause of malaria deaths. There are three main types of tests. Blood smear microscopy examines a blood sample under a microscope and is the most reliable way to confirm infection and identify which species is involved. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) detect small fragments of the parasite and can give results in under 15 minutes, which is useful when microscopy isn't readily available, but they are less sensitive and any RDT result should be confirmed with microscopy. PCR (polymerase chain reaction) testing is the most sensitive option and can confirm the exact parasite species when microscopy can't, which helps guide treatment choice, though results take longer, making PCR less suited to guiding an initial treatment decision. If a test comes back positive, treatment with species-specific medication begins immediately; if negative, the provider will look into other causes for the symptoms.
malaria.travel_prevention: Before traveling to an area where malaria spreads, discuss your detailed itinerary with a healthcare provider -- including specific destinations, accommodation type, season, travel style, pregnancy status, other medical conditions and medications, and known drug resistance patterns at the destination -- so they can recommend the right preventive medication (an antimalarial) and confirm whether it needs to start before departure. Preventive medication must be taken exactly as prescribed, including for the period before travel and after returning, since stopping early can leave a traveler unprotected. People who grew up in or previously lived in a malaria-affected area still need the same precautions as any other traveler -- any natural immunity fades quickly once someone has been away, even briefly. Travelers should buy all antimalarial medication before leaving their home country, since counterfeit or substandard drugs are sold in some countries where malaria spreads and may not work. Preventing mosquito bites remains essential even while taking preventive medication, since no single method is completely effective alone -- use an EPA-registered repellent containing DEET (which offers the strongest protection), picaridin (also called icaridin or KBR 3023), IR3535, or oil of lemon eucalyptus, and combine this with the general mosquito-bite precautions already covered under Prevention. There is currently no vaccine available for general travelers in the United States, though a small number of malaria vaccines have been recommended by WHO specifically for childhood immunization programs in parts of Africa with high transmission. Beyond repellents, additional active ingredients recognized as effective include para-menthane-diol (PMD) and 2-undecanone. Treating clothing and gear (such as boots, pants, socks, and tents) with a 0.5% permethrin spray, or buying pre-treated permethrin clothing, adds another layer of protection -- though permethrin should never be applied directly to skin. Sleeping in a well-screened or air-conditioned room, or under a permethrin-treated bed net, is recommended when other protections aren't available. Importantly, even the best prevention isn't 100% effective: anyone who develops a fever or flu-like illness either while traveling in a malaria-affected area or after returning home -- for up to a full year afterward -- should seek immediate medical attention and be sure to tell the provider about their travel history. Travelers who have recently visited an area where malaria is widespread should also check blood donation eligibility guidelines before donating blood.
malaria.areas_at_risk: Malaria transmission depends heavily on climate, since both the Anopheles mosquito and the malaria parasite's development inside it need warmth to survive -- the parasite's growth cycle in the mosquito is even called its 'extrinsic incubation period.' Below about 20C (68F), Plasmodium falciparum (the parasite behind severe malaria) can't complete this cycle, so it doesn't spread in cooler climates. As a result, malaria is typically found in tropical and subtropical regions, and even within those regions it's usually absent at very high altitudes, in deserts (aside from oases), during colder seasons in some areas, and in countries where successful control or elimination programs have interrupted transmission. Transmission tends to be most intense and year-round in warmer areas closer to the equator. Most cases occur in sub-Saharan Africa, but malaria is also present in parts of Oceania (including Papua New Guinea), Central and South America, and Southeast Asia.

typhoid.name: Typhoid Fever
typhoid.source: World Health Organization — Typhoid fever fact sheet
key_facts: As of 2019 estimates, about 9 million people fall sick with typhoid and roughly 110,000 die from it each year.
It is caused by the bacterium Salmonella Typhi, usually spread through contaminated food or water.
Growing antibiotic resistance is making treatment more complicated in many regions.
A typhoid conjugate vaccine is recommended for children from 6 months of age and adults up to 45 or 65 years, depending on the vaccine.
typhoid.overview: Typhoid fever is a potentially life-threatening bacterial infection. Once ingested, Salmonella Typhi bacteria multiply and spread into the bloodstream. It remains a public health concern where access to safe water and sanitation is limited, and children face the highest risk.
typhoid.escalation_note: Severe, untreated cases can lead to serious complications or death, so persistent high fever with these symptoms should prompt medical evaluation and blood testing to confirm diagnosis.
prevention: Drink only safe water — boiled, filtered, or from a trusted sealed source
Ensure food is properly cooked and served hot
Avoid raw milk or unpasteurized dairy products
Avoid ice unless made from safe water
Wash hands thoroughly and frequently, especially after using the toilet
Wash (and where possible peel) fruits and vegetables before eating raw
Get vaccinated, particularly in high-risk or endemic areas
typhoid.treatment: Typhoid is treated with a full prescribed course of antibiotics — stopping early risks relapse and continued spread, since bacteria can still be shed in stool even after symptoms resolve. Good hand hygiene during recovery, and avoiding food preparation for others, helps prevent passing the infection on. A doctor should confirm the infection has fully cleared through follow-up testing.

cdc_key_points: Typhoid fever and paratyphoid fever are life-threatening illnesses.
Each of the illnesses is caused by a kind of Salmonella bacteria (germs).
Most people in the United States with these illnesses were infected during international travel.
You can find out if you need a typhoid fever vaccine at www.cdc.gov/travel.

germs_responsible.overview: The illnesses are caused by Salmonella bacteria.

illness_estimates.overview: Every year, millions of people around the world get sick from these diseases.

typhoid_fever.worldwide: 9.2 million illnesses are estimated to occur worldwide each year.
typhoid_fever.united_states: 5,700 illnesses and 620 hospitalizations are estimated to occur in the United States each year. Most people are infected while traveling internationally.

paratyphoid_fever.worldwide: 3.8 million illnesses are estimated to occur worldwide each year.
paratyphoid_fever.united_states: CDC does not have estimates of illnesses and hospitalizations in the United States.

where_illness_is_common.overview: These illnesses are most common in parts of the world where water and food can be unsafe, and sanitation can be poor, including parts of:
where_illness_is_common.note: Most people in the United States with typhoid fever or paratyphoid fever were infected while traveling to these places.

risk_factors_detailed.overview: The chances of getting typhoid fever or paratyphoid fever in the United States are very low. The chances increase for people in the United States who:
risk_factors: Travel to countries in Africa, Asia, or Latin America where these diseases are common
Visit rural areas of those countries
Visit family and friends in those countries
Are not vaccinated against typhoid fever
risk_factors_detailed.travel_note: Almost all people in the United States with these diseases report that they have traveled internationally. Most report that they traveled to countries in South Asia, including Pakistan, India, or Bangladesh.

how_it_spreads.overview: The bacteria that cause these illnesses are shed (gotten rid of) in poop.
who_sheds_bacteria: People who have symptoms of typhoid fever or paratyphoid fever
People who are no longer sick but still have the bacteria in their body
how_it_spreads.how_infection_occurs: You can get typhoid fever or paratyphoid fever after swallowing the bacteria. The bacteria can get in your mouth in several ways, including through food, drinks, and water that have been contaminated by sewage, and through food that has been rinsed in contaminated water and then eaten.

fever: The fever can be as high as 103–104°F (39–40°C).
The fever usually lasts more than 3 days.
symptom_details.rash_note: Some people get a rash with flat, rose-colored spots.

seek_care.warning: Do not wait — see a doctor if you have a fever and feel very ill.
seek_care.travel_note: If you are traveling outside the United States and need help finding healthcare, visit CDC's page for getting healthcare during travel.

treatment_importance.you_can_get_very_ill: Without treatment, your fever can last for weeks or months. You also can develop other health problems. These health problems can be very dangerous and might lead to death.
treatment_importance.danger_after_symptoms_fade: If your symptoms go away without treatment, you might still carry the bacteria that made you sick, and it can spread to others or cause your illness to return.

prevention_detailed.overview: Typhoid fever and paratyphoid fever are common in many countries. These countries can have poor sanitation and unsafe water and food.
two_basic_steps: Get a typhoid vaccination before your trip.
Practice safe eating and drinking habits during your trip.

xdr_warning.title: Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) typhoid fever in Pakistan
xdr_warning.details: All travelers to Pakistan are at risk of getting XDR typhoid fever. XDR typhoid fever does not respond to most antibiotics used to treat the disease. Travelers to Pakistan and neighboring countries should get vaccinated before travel and practice safe eating and drinking habits during travel.

why_it_matters: Available vaccines do not protect against paratyphoid fever.
Safe eating and drinking habits also help protect you from other illnesses, including travelers' diarrhea, cholera, and hepatitis A.
wash_your_hands: Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water, especially after using the bathroom and before preparing food or eating.
Use hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol if soap and water are not available.
boil_it_cook_it_peel_it_or_forget_it: Drink unopened, factory-sealed bottled water or boil water for at least 1 minute before using it.
Avoid ice, popsicles, and flavored ices unless they are made from unopened, factory-sealed bottled water or water that was boiled for 1 minute before using it.
Eat only well-cooked foods that are still hot and steaming.
Avoid raw vegetables and fruits that can't be peeled — lettuce and other greens can stay contaminated even if washed.
Avoid food and drinks from street vendors unless they are steaming hot when served.
Drink pasteurized milk from a factory-sealed bottle.

vaccine.overview: Vaccination can help prevent typhoid fever. Find out if you need a typhoid vaccine at www.cdc.gov/travel. Visit a doctor or travel clinic at least 4 weeks before you travel. Two typhoid vaccines are available in the United States: an oral vaccine and an injectable vaccine.

oral_vaccine.who_can_take_it: People who are 6 years or older

injectable_vaccine.who_can_take_it: People who are 2 years or older

vaccine.boosters_note: Typhoid vaccines lose effectiveness (strength) over time. If you were vaccinated in the past, ask your doctor if you need a booster vaccine.

cdc_treatment_details.overview: Antibiotics are used to treat typhoid fever and paratyphoid fever. Timely treatment can help prevent serious health problems. If you are sick, you can help protect others from getting sick too.
cdc_treatment_details.antibiotics_help: Antibiotics can help you recover faster. They also can help lower the risk of complications and death.
cdc_treatment_details.reminder: Use antibiotics only when needed and take them exactly as prescribed. Talk with your healthcare provider if you have any questions about your antibiotics.

antibiotic_resistance.overview: Antibiotic resistance is increasing in bacteria that cause typhoid fever and paratyphoid fever.
antibiotic_resistance.what_is_it: Antibiotic resistance happens when bacteria develop the ability to defeat the drugs designed to kill them. That means they are not killed and continue to grow. Antibiotic-resistant infections can be harder to treat, last longer, cause more severe illness, and lead to higher healthcare costs.
antibiotic_resistance.how_it_affects_treatment: Your healthcare provider might order special tests to see if the bacteria causing your infection are resistant to antibiotics. Results from those tests might affect the antibiotics you receive.

protecting_others.overview: The bacteria that cause typhoid fever and paratyphoid fever can spread easily among people.
protecting_others.work_restrictions: Some people may not be able to return to work until a doctor says they no longer carry the bacteria. These people include healthcare workers, food handlers, and childcare workers.
protecting_others.take_all_antibiotics: Take antibiotics exactly as prescribed. Keep taking them for as long as your healthcare provider says to take them.

tuberculosis.name: Tuberculosis (TB)
tuberculosis.source: World Health Organization — Tuberculosis fact sheet
key_facts: TB caused an estimated 1.23 million deaths in 2024, making it the world's leading cause of death from a single infectious agent.
An estimated 10.7 million people fell ill with TB worldwide in 2024.
Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) remains a serious concern — only about 2 in 5 people with drug-resistant TB accessed treatment in 2024.
TB is both preventable and curable; global efforts have saved an estimated 83 million lives since 2000.
tuberculosis.overview: TB is a bacterial infection that most often affects the lungs and spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or spits. About a quarter of the world's population is estimated to carry TB bacteria, but most people with this latent infection feel fine and aren't contagious — only around 5–10% go on to develop active TB disease. Risk of active disease is higher with diabetes, HIV or other causes of weakened immunity, undernutrition, tobacco use, or heavy alcohol use.
symptoms: Cough lasting several weeks, sometimes with blood
tuberculosis.escalation_note: Symptoms can stay mild for months, which means a person can unknowingly spread TB to others — anyone with a persistent cough, unexplained weight loss, or ongoing fever should get evaluated rather than wait it out.
prevention: Seek medical attention promptly for a prolonged cough, fever, or unexplained weight loss
Get screened if at higher risk (e.g. HIV-positive, or in close contact with someone who has TB)
Complete the full course if prescribed TB preventive treatment
Practice respiratory hygiene — cover coughs, wear a mask if infectious, dispose of tissues properly
Ensure good ventilation in shared indoor spaces
BCG vaccination is given to infants in many countries to reduce risk of severe childhood TB
tuberculosis.treatment: Active TB is treated with a combination of antibiotics (commonly rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) taken daily for 4–6 months. Stopping treatment early is dangerous, as it can allow the bacteria to become drug-resistant. Multidrug-resistant TB requires different, more expensive medicines with more side effects; a newer, shorter 6-month all-oral regimen is now recommended for eligible patients.

tuberculosis_in_india.overview: Tuberculosis in India is a major health problem, causing about 220,000 deaths every year. In 2020, the Indian government made statements to eliminate tuberculosis from the country by 2025 through its National TB Elimination Program. Interventions in this program include major investment in health care, providing supplemental nutrition credit through the Nikshay Poshan Yojana, organizing a national epidemiological survey for tuberculosis, and organizing a national campaign to tie together the Indian government and private health infrastructure for the goal of eliminating the disease. India bears a disproportionately large burden of the world's tuberculosis rates, with WHO statistics for 2022 estimating 2.8 million new infections annually, accounting for 26% of the global total. It is estimated that approximately 40% of the population of India carry tuberculosis infection. The cost of this death and disease to the Indian economy between 2006 and 2014 was approximately US$1 billion.

epidemiology.overview: Tuberculosis is one of India's major public health problems. According to WHO estimates, India has the world's largest tuberculosis epidemic. In 2020, India accounted for 26% of the incident TB cases across the globe, with an incidence rate of 192 cases per 100,000 of population. India accounted for 38% of global TB deaths among HIV-negative people and for 34% of the combined total number of TB deaths in HIV-negative and HIV-positive people. Further in 2020, India accounted for 24% of the global gap between estimated TB incidence and the number of people newly diagnosed with TB and reported.
epidemiology.tdr_tb_findings: A report by Zarir Udwadia, originating from studies at the Hinduja Hospital in Mumbai, discusses drug-resistant TB effects and results. An experiment was conducted in January 2012 on four patients to test how resistant and unique the 'new category' of Totally Drug-Resistant TB (TDR-TB) is. These patients were given all the first-line and second-line drugs usually prescribed to treat tuberculosis and were resistant to all of them. In response, the government of India appeared to stay in denial, while the WHO decided that although patterns of drug-resistance were evident, there was insufficient evidence to create a new category of TDR-TB from these results.
epidemiology.scale_and_trends: Compared to India, Canada has about 1,600 new cases of TB every year. Citing studies of TB-drug sales, the government of India now suggests the total has gone from being 2.2 million to 2.6 million people nationwide. On March 24, 2019 (TB Day), the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare of India notified that 2.15 million new tuberculosis patients were discovered only in 2018. In India, tuberculosis is responsible for the death of every third AIDS patient. Moreover, India accounts for about a quarter of the global tuberculosis burden. The ministry reiterated their commitment to eliminating tuberculosis in the country by 2025. As part of its efforts to eliminate tuberculosis, the Union Government changed the name of Revised National Tuberculosis Control Program (RNTCP) to National Tuberculosis Elimination Program (NTEP) on December 30, 2019.

cause_and_symptoms.bacterium: The bacterium that causes TB is called Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A person can unknowingly acquire this bacteria and have it lie dormant within them, a condition known as inactive (latent) tuberculosis. Active tuberculosis begins when the bacteria starts developing, and the signs and symptoms begin to be visible. Although the TB bacteria can infect any organ (e.g., kidney, lymph nodes, bones, joints), it primarily affects the lungs.
common_symptoms: Coughing that lasts longer than 3 weeks, with green, yellow, or bloody sputum

additional_causes_and_risk_context.weak_immune_system: Susceptibility to tuberculosis is heightened by a weak immune system. That is why babies, children, and senior adults have a higher risk of developing TB. The bacterium spreads in the air sacs and passes into the lungs. Coughing, sneezing, and even talking to someone can release the mycobacterium into the air, and a person's chances of becoming infected are higher in countries where TB is common and where there is a big proportion of homeless people — India, having the most TB cases of any country, clearly falls into this category.
additional_causes_and_risk_context.socioeconomic_dimensions: Local decreases in the incidence of tuberculosis in India correlate with improvements in social and economic determinants of health more than with access to quality treatment. In India, pollution is widespread throughout the country. Pollution causes many effects in the air that people breathe, and since TB can be passed from person to person through the air, the chances of catching TB remain high in many parts of India.
additional_causes_and_risk_context.lack_of_infrastructure: Another major cause for the growth of TB in India has to do with its standing as a developing country. A study of Delhi slums has shown that lower scores on the Human Development Index and high proportions of one-room dwellings tend to correlate with TB at higher rates. Poorly built environments, including hazards in the workplace, poor ventilation, and overcrowded homes, have also been found to increase exposure to TB.
additional_causes_and_risk_context.lack_of_access_to_treatment: A major reason for the high incidence of TB in India is that the majority of those infected are not able to afford the treatment drugs prescribed. At present, only about 1.5 million patients already under the Indian government's care get free treatments for regular TB, leaving patients who seek treatment in India's growing private sector to buy drugs for themselves — most struggle to do that. Although the Revised National Tuberculosis Control Program (RNTCP) has focused on increasing access to TB care for poor people, the majority of poor people still cannot access TB care financially. It is estimated that just 16% of patients with drug-resistant TB are receiving appropriate treatment. To combat this, India has begun a program to try to provide free drugs to all those infected in the country. While RNTCP has created schemes to offer free or subsidized, high-quality TB care, less than 1% of private practitioners have become fully involved, exacerbated by a lack of education and background information among practitioners about prescribing drugs. A study conducted in Mumbai by Udwadia, Amale, Ajbani, and Rodrigues showed that only 5 of 106 private practitioners practicing in a crowded area called Dharavi could give a correct prescription for a hypothetical patient with MDR-TB. Because the majority of TB cases are treated by private providers, and because the majority of poor people access informal (private) providers, the RNTCP's goals for universal access to TB care may have difficulty being met.
additional_causes_and_risk_context.poor_health: Poverty and a lack of financial resources are also associated with malnutrition, poor housing conditions, substance misuse, and HIV/AIDS incidence. These factors often contribute to a weakened immune system and are accordingly correlated with a higher susceptibility to TB, and tend to have a greater impact on people from high-incidence countries such as India. Indeed, addressing these factors may have a stronger correlation with decreased TB incidence than removing the financial burdens associated with care. Yet, the RNTCP's treatment protocols do not address these social determinants of health.

treatment_in_india.overview: Although tuberculosis is on the rise in India, treatment for it is also on the rise. To prevent spreading TB, it is important to get help quickly and to follow the treatment from a doctor through to completion — this can stop transmission of the bacteria and the appearance of antibiotic-resistant strains. The antibiotics most commonly used include isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.
treatment_in_india.ntep_regimen: The treatment under the National TB Elimination Program (NTEP) in India consists of a 2(HRZE)/4(HRE) anti-TB regime, wherein isoniazid (INH), rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol are given for an initial two months (intensive phase), followed by four months of INH, rifampicin, and ethambutol. This treatment is a daily fixed-dose combination-based regime. It is crucial for a patient to take the medication their doctor prescribes and to continue taking it for the full course of treatment (which may last months or even years) to help ward off antibiotic-resistant types of TB bacteria, which take longer and are more difficult to treat.
treatment_in_india.drug_resistant_tb_note: In India, the majority of infections resistant to regular antibiotic treatment (MDR-TB, XDR-TB, TDR-TB) require, rather than one or two medications, a combination of different medications prescribed over a course of between 18 and 24 months, depending on how deep the infection is. Since the 1960s, isoniazid and rifampicin have been the standard TB treatment.
treatment_in_india.vaccine_note: A vaccine (BCG) is available to limit the spread of bacteria after TB infection. This vaccine is generally used in countries or communities where the risk of TB infection is greater than 1% each year, which includes parts of India.
treatment_in_india.ntep_program_scope: In the past, treatment modalities in the public sector in India did have some drawbacks. However, recently there has been significant improvement in TB healthcare services in the public sector. The NTEP has broadened its spectrum, in addition to providing free diagnostic and treatment services for drug-sensitive and drug-resistant forms of tuberculosis. The program is currently also targeting TB preventive therapy in vulnerable populations with TB infection who are at increased risk of progressing to active TB disease.
treatment_in_india.private_sector_quality_issues: 70-80% of TB patients first visit the private sector, where the diagnostic and treatment services for TB are suboptimal and need to be improved. Quantified by the PRAMAN India study, 53.3% of anti-TB prescriptions prescribed in non-programmatic (private) settings in India are estimated to be incorrect. Similarly, the burden of incorrect anti-TB prescriptions has been estimated by the study to be 2.06 million annually, which translates to 5 incorrect anti-TB prescriptions per minute.
treatment_in_india.adherence_support: Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) has been helpful in increasing adherence and reducing resistance. In recent years, as smartphone usage and accessibility to low-cost internet services have gained traction in India, alternative services such as SMS reminders, voice calls, and video DOT (vDOT) have been explored and shown to be acceptable to a variety of patient populations, thus saving time and money.

history_in_india.overview: India's response to TB has changed with time and with the increasing sophistication of technology. Responses to TB have evolved from pre-independence, through post-independence, to the current WHO-assisted period. The first national study of tuberculosis in India was carried out by Arthur Lankester in 1914.
history_in_india.rntcp: Following independence, the Indian government established various regional and national TB reduction programmes. The Indian government's Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) started in India in 1997. The program used the WHO-recommended Directly Observed Treatment Short Course (DOTS) strategy to develop ideas and data on TB treatment. This group's initial objective was to achieve and maintain a TB treatment success rate of at least 85% in India among new patients. In 2010, the RNTCP made a major policy decision to change focus and adopt the concept of Universal Access to quality diagnosis and TB treatment for all TB patients, offering a helping hand to all people diagnosed with TB by providing better quality services and improvement in therapy.
history_in_india.contemporary_response: The contemporary response to TB includes India's participation and leadership in global TB reduction and elimination programs. Treatment recommendations from Udwadia et al. suggest that patients with TDR-TB should only be treated within the confines of government-sanctioned DOTS-Plus Programs to prevent the emergence of this untreatable form of tuberculosis. Given this conclusion, it was considered certain, as of 2012, that the new Indian government program would insist on providing drugs free of charge to TB patients in India for the first time ever.

society_and_culture_india.organizations: The Tuberculosis Association of India is a voluntary organization that was set up in February 1939. It is affiliated with the government of India and works with the TB Delhi center.
society_and_culture_india.laboratories: The RNTCP has established a network of laboratories where TB tests can be done for purposes of diagnosis and to determine whether a person has drug-resistant TB. The laboratory system comprises the National Reference Laboratories (NRLs), state-level Intermediate Reference Laboratories (IRLs), Culture & Drug Susceptibility Testing (C&DST) laboratories, and Designated Microscopy Centres (DMCs). Some private laboratories are also accredited as Culture & Drug Susceptibility Testing laboratories for tuberculosis (e.g., Microcare Laboratory & Tuberculosis Research Centre, Surat).
society_and_culture_india.stigma: Disempowerment and stigma are often experienced by TB patients, as they are disproportionately impoverished or socially marginalized. The DOTS treatment regimen of the RNTCP is thought to deepen this sentiment, as its close monitoring of patients can lead to stigma. To counteract disempowerment, some countries have engaged patients in the process of implementing DOTS and in creating other treatment regimens that give more attention to their nonclinical needs. Pro-poor strategies — including wage compensation for time lost to treatment, working with civil society organizations to link low-income patients to social services and nutritional support, and offering local NGOs and committees a platform for engagement with the work done by private providers — may reduce the burden of TB and lead to greater patient autonomy.
society_and_culture_india.economics_note: Some legal advocates have argued that public interest litigation in India must be part of the TB response strategy to ensure that available resources actually fund the necessary health response, given India's large share of the world's TB burden.

diabetes.name: Diabetes
diabetes.source: World Health Organization — Diabetes fact sheet
key_facts: The number of people living with diabetes rose from 200 million in 1990 to 830 million in 2022, rising faster in low- and middle-income countries.
More than half of people with diabetes were not taking medication for it in 2022.
Diabetes can cause blindness, kidney failure, heart attack, stroke, and lower-limb amputation.
In 2021, diabetes and related kidney disease caused over 2 million deaths, and about 11% of cardiovascular deaths were linked to high blood glucose.
A healthy diet, regular activity, a healthy body weight, and avoiding tobacco can prevent or delay type 2 diabetes.
diabetes.overview: Diabetes is a chronic condition where the pancreas doesn't produce enough insulin, or the body can't use the insulin it produces effectively. This leads to raised blood glucose (hyperglycaemia), which over time damages nerves and blood vessels throughout the body. Type 1 diabetes requires daily insulin and has no known prevention. Type 2 diabetes makes up more than 95% of cases, is often preventable, and is linked to excess weight, low physical activity, and genetics. Gestational diabetes occurs during pregnancy and raises future type 2 risk for both mother and child.
symptoms: Needing to urinate more often than usual
diabetes.escalation_note: Type 2 diabetes symptoms are often mild and can go unnoticed for years, sometimes only diagnosed after complications have already developed — which is why regular checkups and blood tests matter even without obvious symptoms.
prevention: Maintain a healthy body weight
Get at least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity per week
Eat a balanced diet, limiting sugar and saturated fat
Avoid tobacco use
Get regular checkups and blood glucose testing, especially with a family history of diabetes
diabetes.treatment: Diagnosis is done through blood glucose testing. Type 1 diabetes requires daily insulin injections for survival. Type 2 diabetes is managed through lifestyle changes, and sometimes medication such as metformin, sulfonylureas, or SGLT-2 inhibitors, occasionally alongside insulin. People with diabetes may also need blood-pressure medication, statins, regular foot care, kidney disease screening, and eye exams to catch complications early.

diabd_bangladesh_dataset.source_note: Data in Brief (ScienceDirect) — 'DiaBD: A dataset for enhanced risk analysis and research in Bangladesh'
diabd_bangladesh_dataset.abstract_summary: Diabetes is a chronic condition affecting millions worldwide and severely impacts health and quality of life. According to the International Diabetes Federation (IDF), over 463 million adults, which is 9.3% of the global population, live with diabetes. Diabetes ranks among the most prevalent chronic diseases and was the ninth-leading cause of mortality in 2019, with 4.2 million deaths reported. This article introduces DiaBD, a novel dataset of 5,288 patient records from Bangladesh, designed to address critical gaps in diabetes research and aid in healthcare planning, risk analysis, and predictive modelling. The dataset comprises 14 attributes including age, gender, clinical vitals (pulse rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, glucose levels), anthropometrics (height, weight, body mass index), family history of diabetes and hypertension, cardiovascular disease (CVD), and stroke, with a dependent attribute, Diabetic, indicating whether an individual has diabetes or not.

specifications.subject: Computer Sciences; Health Sciences, Medical Sciences & Pharmacology
specifications.specific_subject_area: Diabetes Data Analysis, Type-2 Diabetes Risk Analysis
specifications.data_collection_summary: Community health workers (CHWs) collected data from 5,288 participants across 63 diverse Bangladeshi Unions using a smart health kit and an AI-based app under the Enriched Sastho program. They gathered categorical and quantitative measures, including vitals like blood pressure and glucose, with tools such as a Sphygmomanometer and Glucometer. The dataset included individuals aged 21-80 years, with incomplete records excluded. Measurements followed WHO guidelines, and the data were validated to ensure the dataset's highest standard.
specifications.data_source_location: CMED Health Ltd. and Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation (PKSF); Country: Bangladesh

data_accessibility.access_note: Publicly available in CSV format with no access controls required.
data_accessibility.license: CC BY 4.0 — free to use with credit; link license, note changes, and no endorsement; third-party content may need permission.

value_of_the_data: The dataset includes key attributes such as blood pressure, glucose levels, BMI, hypertension, stroke, and CVD, providing comprehensive information on diabetes and its complications to enable development of effective preventive and therapeutic measures. The prevalence of diabetes within the dataset is approximately 6.5%, with 342 diabetic individuals out of 5,288 total participants.

The dataset is crucial for developing and validating machine learning algorithms for early diabetes detection, risk assessment, and prediction of disease progression. A Random Forest (RF) classifier trained on the dataset achieved the highest performance with 99.26% accuracy and 0.99 AUC for DiaBD, compared to 85.56% accuracy and 0.84 AUC on the PIMA dataset, and 91.7% accuracy and 0.92 AUC on the Ranchi dataset.

This dataset addresses key research gaps in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) by providing region-specific data that is often underrepresented in global studies. Unlike the PIMA dataset, which focuses only on Pima Indian women, this dataset includes a diverse demographic from urban, semi-urban, and rural areas of Bangladesh, capturing how demographics and medical conditions (e.g., hypertension, CVD) influence outcomes.

The dataset helps design personalized medicine strategies by identifying high-risk individuals based on their health data. Healthcare professionals can use this data to identify trends, design targeted treatment plans, and improve patient care, and it supports the development of predictive models for clinical decision-making.

DiaBD can be reused in health informatics, public health, and epidemiology to study risk factors, intervention strategies, and healthcare analytics, and can be integrated with external data sources to help analyze broader trends in diabetes and its comorbidities in different regions or populations.
diabd_bangladesh_dataset.background: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a metabolic disorder characterized by persistently high blood glucose levels that lead to symptoms like frequent urination, thirst, and hunger. If untreated, DM can cause severe complications such as diabetic ketoacidosis or death, and damage blood vessels, raising the risks of heart attack, stroke, kidney disease, and vision loss. The complexity and wide-ranging impact of diabetes necessitate robust datasets for accurate research and risk assessment. There are problems with existing datasets like the PIMA dataset, the Ranchi University dataset, the Luzhou (China) dataset, and the Reza et al. dataset — these include small sample sizes, poor demographic representation, and limited clinical or lifestyle parameters.

diabd_bangladesh_dataset.demographic_and_health_condition_breakdo: The dataset includes 70.95% female and 29.05% male participants. Regarding age distribution, the percentages for the age groups 21-29 years, 30-39 years, 40-49 years, 50-59 years, and over 60 years are 7.31%, 28.93%, 21.70%, 21.56%, and 20.16% respectively — the most significant proportion is in the 30-39 years range, followed by 40-49 and 50-59 years, with smaller proportions in the 21-29 and 60+ years groups. In terms of health conditions, 11.10% of patients are hypertensive, while 88.90% are not. The dataset also includes 0.38% of patients with a history of stroke and 1.13% with cardiovascular disease. Regarding medical history, 3.20% of patients report having a close relative with type 2 diabetes, and 3.76% have one or both parents diagnosed with hypertension.

experimental_design_and_methods.overview: The study involved 5,288 participants, carefully selected to represent a diverse Bangladeshi population across various ages, sexes, socioeconomic statuses, and geographic locations.
experimental_design_and_methods.limitations_of_existing_datasets: Datasets like PIMA often lack demographic diversity among participants, leading to the overrepresation of some groups and the exclusion of others. The PIMA dataset exclusively focuses on Pima Indian women and lacks representation from males or other ethnic backgrounds. Similarly, datasets from institutions like Ranchi University and Luzhou Hospital exhibit imbalances in gender distribution and lack comprehensive documentation on vital health parameters. These limitations restrict the generalizability and applicability of these datasets in broader research contexts.
experimental_design_and_methods.data_collection_methodology: Data were collected from a study conducted in different regions of Bangladesh, where community health workers (CHWs) used an innovative health kit and an AI-based mobile app to provide weekly health education, screenings, risk assessments, and digital referrals. The study used a repeated cross-sectional design to evaluate the impact of a digital health intervention on health outcomes in rural Bangladesh. Data collection occurred between April 10, 2021, and May 27, 2024, as a joint initiative by CMED Health and PKSF. Data was collected from 5,288 participants across 63 Unions in urban, semi-urban, and rural areas using random selection. CHWs obtained informed written consent from all participants and provided details about the study's nature and risks. CHWs visited each household once a week to collect health vitals and input them into a digital profile through the 'Enriched Sastho' application. Participants aged 21-80 years were selected, as this is the most crucial age group for Type 2 diabetes (T2D) in Bangladesh. According to a recent study, the prevalence of T2D was 10.8% in urban areas and 7.4% in rural areas, with 31.4% of the urban population and 27% of the rural population affected by pre-diabetes; participants were distributed across urban, semi-urban, and rural areas according to this population distribution to maintain demographic balance, and were randomly selected within the age group. The selected areas also had a higher concentration of migrations of populations from various regions across the country. The study used a triangulation of quantitative, qualitative, and participant-observation methods, following Action Research principles. It was initially conducted as a pilot project on digital health services in a union consisting of 21 villages of the Dhamrai sub-district, Dhaka, Bangladesh. CHWs were trained according to WHO guidelines for non-communicable diseases and received three months of training before data collection with a government-approved training module. Inter-rater reliability was ensured through this standardized training and a pilot test under the supervision of three groups of physicians to confirm consistency in data collection and recording across different areas. To mitigate selection bias, participants were randomly selected in the age range of 21 to 80 years from defined areas, and participants who were not Bangladeshi citizens or did not meet the age criteria were excluded, ensuring a representative sample of the Bangladeshi population.
experimental_design_and_methods.instruments_and_tools: Data were collected using a structured questionnaire, with closed-ended questions for categorical variables and quantitative measures (e.g., blood pressure, glucose levels) utilizing validated instruments approved by CE/FDA included in the CMED health kit. The CMED Health Kit contains tools to measure height (Height Scale), weight (Weight Scale), blood pressure (Sphygmomanometer), blood sugar (Glucometer), blood oxygen saturation (Pulse Oximeter), and temperature (Thermometer). Additionally, it tracks BMI, pulse rate, and uses the MUAC tape to assess nutritional status. The pilot project evaluated the validity of the questionnaire, translated it into Bangla, and verified it through back-translation. CHWs visit participants weekly and collect data on health vitals, including blood pressure, glucose levels, and BMI, during every session, selecting the most frequent and stable values from the collected data for analysis; glucose levels are tested randomly during each session. After data collection, three teams of physicians reviewed the data to ensure it met WHO standards, confirming its accuracy and reliability for analysis.
experimental_design_and_methods.data_preprocessing: Error correction and data cleaning were performed to remove inaccuracies and noise from the dataset. Initially, duplicate records were identified and removed from an initial dataset of 5,373, resulting in 5,301 unique records. Patient cases with missing data for any attributes were then excluded to ensure the integrity and consistency of the dataset, which reduced it to 5,288 records. Despite the varied data collection settings, each CHW followed the same protocol, measurement techniques, and tools to maintain data consistency. Biometric measurements (including blood pressure, glucose levels, and BMI) and categorical data (such as gender labels and hypertension status) were standardized to maintain uniformity across the dataset. To maintain the raw form of the dataset, flexibility was allowed for applying normalization techniques based on specific analytical needs; consistent measurement techniques and tools were used across all settings to achieve reliable data.
experimental_design_and_methods.technical_validation: A collaborative validation protocol ensured the accuracy and reliability of the diabetes-related dataset through a two-stage process designed to meet clinical standards and ensure clinical validity. The protocol included three independent groups of physicians from diverse medical backgrounds. If two teams agreed on a diabetic or non-diabetic classification, they finalized that without further review. In cases of disagreement, they escalated the flagged entries to a third group of physicians, who impartially reviewed the discrepancies and made the final, clinically valid recommendations, correcting and confirming errors and retaining valid entries that were initially flagged as errors. This structured, consensus-driven validation framework bolstered the robustness and clinical reliability of the dataset.

diabd_bangladesh_dataset.limitations: The dataset exhibits some imbalances; for instance, there are more participants without diabetes than with diabetes. Furthermore, there is a gender imbalance, with female participants almost twice as many as male participants. These imbalances will introduce statistical bias and may affect the generalizability and accuracy of the findings. The data was curated thoroughly, but there are biases and a lack of representation, which are critical factors that will affect the overall reliability of the study.
diabd_bangladesh_dataset.ethics_statement: The data collection and validation process adhered to ethical standards, with protocols approved by the ethical review board of United International University (UIU) (Reference No: IREB/2023/009). Robust security measures were implemented to protect all personal data and prevent unauthorized access. Informed written consent was obtained from all participants, who were fully informed about the nature of the study, potential risks, and their rights to withdraw at any time. They voluntarily agreed to participate after having all aspects of the study explained to them. To protect participant rights and dignity, the researchers meticulously observed all ethical considerations throughout the study, including confidentiality, anonymity, and responsible sharing of data to maintain the highest ethical standards.

influenza.name: Seasonal Influenza (Flu)
influenza.source: World Health Organization — Seasonal influenza fact sheet
key_facts: There are roughly one billion cases of seasonal influenza every year, including 3–5 million severe cases.
It causes an estimated 290,000 to 650,000 respiratory deaths annually worldwide.
Around 99% of deaths in children under 5 from flu-related lower respiratory infections occur in developing countries.
Symptoms typically begin 1–4 days after infection and last about a week.
influenza.overview: Seasonal influenza is a common, highly contagious respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses, spreading easily through coughing, sneezing, and contaminated hands. Most people recover without needing medical treatment, and vaccination remains the most effective way to prevent it.
influenza.escalation_note: While most cases resolve on their own, influenza can occasionally lead to pneumonia or sepsis, especially in high-risk groups — anyone with worsening symptoms or an existing chronic condition should seek medical care rather than wait it out.
prevention: Get an annual flu vaccination, especially if in a high-risk group
Wash hands regularly
Cover your mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing
Dispose of used tissues properly
Stay home when feeling unwell
Avoid close contact with sick people
Avoid touching your eyes, nose, or mouth
influenza.treatment: Most people recover with rest, fluids, and symptom relief, and should stay home to avoid spreading the virus further. People in high-risk groups or with severe symptoms should be treated with antiviral medication promptly and seek medical care if symptoms worsen.
additional_sources: U.S. CDC — Signs and Symptoms of Flu
U.S. CDC — Seasonal Flu and Staph Infection
U.S. CDC — How Flu Spreads
influenza.cdc_about: Influenza (also known as "flu") is a contagious respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses. It can cause mild to severe illness, and at times can lead to death.
cdc_symptoms: Some people may have vomiting and diarrhea, though this is more common in children than adults
influenza.cdc_symptoms_note: Flu symptoms usually come on suddenly. *It's important to note that not everyone with flu will have a fever.
influenza.cdc_complications: Most people who get flu will recover in a few days to less than two weeks, but some people will develop complications (such as pneumonia) as a result of flu, some of which can be life-threatening and result in death. Sinus and ear infections are examples of moderate complications from flu, while pneumonia is a serious flu complication that can result from either flu virus infection alone or from co-infection of flu virus and bacteria. Other possible serious complications triggered by flu can include inflammation of the heart (myocarditis), brain (encephalitis) or muscle tissues (myositis, rhabdomyolysis), and multi-organ failure (for example, respiratory and kidney failure). Flu virus infection of the respiratory tract can trigger an extreme inflammatory response in the body and can lead to sepsis, the body's life-threatening response to infection. Flu also can make chronic medical problems worse — for example, people with asthma may experience asthma attacks while they have flu, and people with chronic heart disease may experience a worsening of this condition triggered by flu.
influenza.cdc_higher_risk_groups: Anyone can get sick with flu, even healthy people, and serious problems related to flu can happen to anyone at any age, but some people are at higher risk of developing serious flu-related complications if they get sick. This includes people 65 years and older, people of any age with certain chronic medical conditions (such as asthma, diabetes, or heart disease), pregnant women, and children younger than 5 years, but especially those younger than 2 years old.

cdc_emergency_warning_signs.note: People experiencing these warning signs should obtain medical care right away.
in_children: Ribs pulling in with each breath
Severe muscle pain (child refuses to walk)
Dehydration (no urine for 8 hours, dry mouth, no tears when crying)
Not alert or interacting when awake
Fever above 104 degrees Fahrenheit that is not controlled by fever-reducing medicine
In children younger than 12 weeks, any fever
in_adults: Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath
Persistent pain or pressure in the chest or abdomen
Persistent dizziness, confusion, inability to arouse
Fever or cough that improve but then return or worsen

cdc_seasonal_flu_and_staph_infection.background: Staphylococcus aureus, often referred to simply as "staph," are bacteria commonly carried on the skin or in the nose of healthy people. Staph bacteria frequently cause skin infections, such as boils; most of these infections are not life-threatening. In addition to skin infections, staph bacteria can cause infections in the blood, in the bones, and in the lungs (pneumonia). In the past, most serious staph bacterial infections could be treated with an antibiotic related to penicillin. However, over the past 50 years, some staph bacteria have become resistant to antibiotics, including the commonly used penicillin-related antibiotics — these resistant staph bacteria are called methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, or MRSA.
cdc_seasonal_flu_and_staph_infection.flu_and_mrsa: The overall risk of developing a MRSA infection after flu appears to be very low. However, CDC continues to work with state and local public health authorities to better understand this association. CDC is working with state and local public health authorities to monitor and investigate infections with MRSA, including pneumonias and other types of MRSA infections that occur in patients with flu. CDC also acts as a technical advisor to state and local health departments and various professional organizations that are working to control MRSA.

key_points: Experts think that influenza viruses spread mainly by droplets made when people with flu cough, sneeze, or talk.
Less often, a person might get influenza (flu) by touching a surface or object that has influenza virus on it and then touching their own mouth, nose, or possibly their eyes.
Influenza viruses can be detected in most infected people beginning one day before symptoms develop and up to five to seven days after becoming sick.
People with flu are the most contagious during the first three days of their illness.
cdc_how_flu_spreads.why_it_spreads: People with flu can spread it to others. Most experts think that influenza viruses spread mainly by droplets made when people with flu cough, sneeze, or talk. These droplets can land in the mouths or noses of people who are nearby or possibly be inhaled into the lungs. Putting physical distance between yourself and others can help lower the risk of spreading or catching flu.

chikungunya.name: Chikungunya
chikungunya.source: World Health Organization — Chikungunya fact sheet
key_facts: Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne viral disease, with large outbreaks and sporadic cases reported mainly across the Americas, Asia, and Africa.
Its symptoms closely resemble dengue and Zika, which often leads to misdiagnosis.
It causes fever and often severe, sometimes prolonged, joint pain.
Two vaccines have received regulatory approval in some countries but are not yet in widespread use.
Severe symptoms and deaths are rare, occurring mostly in very young infants or older adults with existing health conditions.
chikungunya.overview: Chikungunya is caused by the chikungunya virus (CHIKV) and is transmitted by the same Aedes mosquitoes responsible for spreading dengue — mainly Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus — which bite primarily during the day. The disease's name comes from a Kimakonde word describing the contorted, stooped posture caused by severe joint pain.
chikungunya.symptom_onset: Symptoms typically begin 4–8 days (range 2–12 days) after an infected mosquito bite. Joint pain often lasts a few days but can persist for weeks, months, or occasionally longer. Most people recover fully.
chikungunya.escalation_note: Newborns and older adults with existing health conditions face higher risk of severe disease and should seek medical care if symptoms are severe; rare eye, heart, or neurological complications have been reported.
prevention: Wear clothing that minimizes skin exposure to daytime mosquitoes
Use window and door screens
Apply mosquito repellents containing DEET, IR3535, or icaridin
Use insecticide-treated mosquito nets, especially for daytime sleepers such as young children or the elderly
Empty and clean water-holding containers weekly to eliminate mosquito breeding sites
People already infected should avoid further mosquito bites during their first week of illness to limit spread
chikungunya.treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment. Paracetamol is recommended for fever and pain relief; NSAIDs should be avoided until dengue has been ruled out, since they can increase bleeding risk. Rest and adequate fluids support recovery.
additional_sources: U.S. CDC — About Chikungunya Virus
U.S. CDC — Symptoms of Chikungunya
U.S. CDC — Chikungunya: Causes and How It Spreads
U.S. CDC — Chikungunya Vaccines
U.S. CDC — Preventing Chikungunya
cdc_key_points: Chikungunya virus spreads to people through the bite of an infected mosquito.
Symptoms can include fever, joint pain, headache, muscle pain, joint swelling, and rash.
No medicines are available to treat chikungunya virus disease.
The best way to prevent chikungunya is to prevent mosquito bites and get vaccinated before traveling, if vaccination is recommended for you.

Outbreaks of chikungunya virus have occurred in Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe, and islands in the Indian and Pacific Oceans, and there is a risk the virus can spread to unaffected areas by infected travelers.
chikungunya.symptom_details: Symptoms usually begin 3–7 days after an infected mosquito bites you. Most people infected with chikungunya virus will develop some symptoms. The most common symptoms are fever and joint pain; other symptoms can include headache, muscle pain, joint swelling, and rash.
chikungunya.outcomes_and_complications: Most patients feel better within a week. However, joint pain can be severe and disabling and might persist for months. Death from chikungunya is rare.
risk_factors: Newborns infected around the time of birth
Older adults (65 years and older)
People with medical conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes, or heart disease
chikungunya.about_the_virus: Chikungunya virus belongs to the family Togaviridae, genus Alphavirus. Chikungunya virus particles are enveloped icosahedral capsids with a diameter of 60–70 nm. Alphavirus infections can either cause arthralgic (joint pain) or neuroinvasive (central nervous system) disease. Other medically important alphaviruses found in the Americas include eastern equine encephalitis virus (neuroinvasive), Mayaro virus (arthralgic), and western equine encephalitis virus (neuroinvasive).
chikungunya.transmission_cycle: Chikungunya virus is primarily transmitted to people through the bite of an infected mosquito, mainly Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus. People are the primary hosts of chikungunya virus during epidemic periods. Mosquitoes become infected when they feed on a person who already has the virus. People infected with chikungunya virus have high enough levels of virus in their blood (viremia) during the first week of illness to transmit the virus to mosquitoes; risk of further spread increases if people with viremia are bitten by uninfected mosquitoes. Because of the high level of virus in blood, spread can also occur through blood transfusion (probable) and exposure to the virus in a laboratory setting. The virus does not spread from person to person through coughing, sneezing, or touching. Person-to-person transmission via in utero and intrapartum routes has been documented, and it is likely the virus can also be transmitted via blood transfusions.
chikungunya.pregnancy_and_breastfeeding: Rarely, chikungunya infection can spread from a pregnant woman to her fetus (in utero transmission). If the pregnant woman is infected around the time of delivery, the baby can be infected at birth (intrapartum transmission), often resulting in severe disease in the baby. Chikungunya virus has not been found in breast milk, and there have been no reports to date of infants being infected through breastfeeding. Because the benefits of breastfeeding likely outweigh the risk of spreading the virus through breastfeeding, mothers should continue to breastfeed even if they are infected with chikungunya virus or live in an area with ongoing virus transmission.
chikungunya.testing_and_diagnosis: See a healthcare provider if you have visited an area where chikungunya virus is found and have symptoms described above. Tell your healthcare provider when and where you traveled. A healthcare provider can order tests to look for chikungunya or other similar viruses like dengue and Zika.

vaccine.name: VIMKUNYA (virus-like particle chikungunya vaccine)
vaccine.availability: Available in the United States as of the CDC's January 23, 2026 update.
vaccine.how_it_works: The vaccine uses a molecule that resembles the virus closely enough to prompt an immune response to help prevent illness. It does not use a live or weakened form of the chikungunya virus.
recommendations: Approved for use in people 12 years and older
Some travelers at higher risk of exposure to chikungunya virus should consider getting vaccinated before their trip
Talk to your healthcare provider if traveling to an area with risk for chikungunya
contraindications_and_precautions: People with a history of a severe allergic reaction to any component of the vaccine should not get vaccinated.
Pregnant women should discuss with a healthcare provider the risks and benefits of the vaccine compared to the risk of chikungunya illness.
People with weakened immune systems might not get as much protection from vaccination.
pre_travel_considerations: Symptoms of chikungunya and possible long-term joint problems after infection
Benefits and possible side effects of vaccination
Outbreaks or ongoing disease activity at your destination
Duration of travel or residence, including likelihood of future travel to an area with chikungunya

cdc_prevention.most_recent_us_case_note: The most recent locally acquired case in the U.S. was reported from a U.S. state in 2025.
prevent_mosquito_bites: Use Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)-registered insect repellent.
Treat clothing and gear with 0.5% permethrin.
Choose lodging with air conditioning or screens on windows and doors; use a mosquito net if sleeping outdoors.
cdc_prevention.areas_note: Chikungunya occurs primarily in Africa, Southeast Asia, the Indian subcontinent, the Pacific Region, and tropical regions of the Americas, but outbreaks have occurred in other locations that have Aedes species mosquitoes that spread the virus. Anyone who spends time in a place where chikungunya occurs is at risk.
cdc_prevention.vaccination_note: In addition to preventing mosquito bites, a chikungunya vaccine may be recommended for travelers going to certain locations. Discuss the need for vaccination with your healthcare provider.

chikungunya.cdc_treatment_details: No medicines are available to treat chikungunya. Rest, fluids, and over-the-counter pain medicines can relieve some symptoms. Take medicine such as acetaminophen or paracetamol to reduce fever and pain. Do not take aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen, until dengue can be ruled out, to reduce the risk of bleeding.

hypertension.name: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure)
hypertension.source: World Health Organization — Hypertension fact sheet
key_facts: An estimated 1.28 billion adults aged 30–79 worldwide have hypertension, about two-thirds of them living in low- and middle-income countries.
Less than half of adults with hypertension (about 42%) are diagnosed and receiving treatment.
Only around 1 in 5 adults with hypertension (about 21%) have it under control.
Hypertension is a major cause of premature death worldwide, largely through its role in heart disease and stroke.
A global target aims to reduce the prevalence of hypertension by 33% between 2010 and 2030.
hypertension.overview: Hypertension is a condition where blood pressure in the arteries stays persistently elevated. It's often called a 'silent' condition because it typically causes no noticeable symptoms, so most people who have it don't know until it's measured or until it leads to a complication such as a heart attack or stroke. Regular blood pressure monitoring is the main way it gets caught early.

modifiable: Unhealthy diet, especially high salt intake
non_modifiable: Co-existing conditions such as diabetes or kidney disease

symptoms: Hypertension usually causes no symptoms at all, which is why routine screening matters even when feeling healthy.
In more severe or advanced cases, some people notice headaches, shortness of breath, nosebleeds, or dizziness — but these are not reliable early warning signs.
hypertension.escalation_note: A very high blood pressure reading (roughly above 180/120 mmHg) accompanied by any of the severe warning signs above is considered a hypertensive emergency and needs immediate medical attention.
prevention: Reduce salt intake in the diet
Maintain a healthy body weight
Exercise regularly
Limit alcohol consumption
Avoid tobacco use
Manage stress
Get blood pressure checked periodically, particularly after age 30 or with a family history of hypertension
hypertension.treatment: Hypertension is managed through a combination of lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, reduced salt and alcohol, no tobacco) and, when needed, blood-pressure-lowering medication prescribed by a doctor. Because it's usually symptom-free, ongoing monitoring and adherence to treatment are essential even when a person feels fine.
