diagnosis.who_diagnoses: A health care team diagnoses high blood pressure and makes treatment decisions by reviewing systolic (first number) and diastolic (second number) blood pressure readings and comparing them to clinical guidelines (ACC/AHA guidelines, in the U.S.).
diagnosis.note: Blood pressure changes throughout the day based on activity; a diagnosis of high blood pressure is usually based on readings that are consistently above normal over time, not a single measurement. Measuring blood pressure is the only way to know whether you have high blood pressure, since it usually causes no symptoms.

causes_detailed: High blood pressure usually develops over time and can occur because of unhealthy lifestyle choices, such as not getting enough regular physical activity.
Certain health conditions, such as diabetes and obesity, can increase the risk for developing high blood pressure.
High blood pressure can also occur during pregnancy.
People who have depression, anxiety, stress, or post-traumatic stress disorder over a long period of time may develop other health problems, including an increased heart rate and high blood pressure.
Other risk factors, such as family history and the environment, can also increase a person's risk for high blood pressure.

complications_detailed.overview: High blood pressure can damage your health in many ways. It can seriously hurt important organs like the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes. In most cases, blood pressure can be managed to lower the risk for these serious health problems.
complications_detailed.heart_attack_and_heart_disease: High blood pressure can damage the arteries by making them less elastic, which decreases the flow of blood and oxygen to the heart and leads to heart disease. Decreased blood flow to the heart can also cause chest pain (angina); a heart attack, which happens when the blood supply to the heart is blocked and heart muscle begins to die without enough oxygen (the longer the blood flow is blocked, the greater the damage); and heart failure, a condition in which the heart can't pump enough blood and oxygen to the other organs.
complications_detailed.stroke_and_brain_problems: High blood pressure can cause the arteries that supply blood and oxygen to the brain to burst or become blocked, causing a stroke. Brain cells die during a stroke because they do not get enough oxygen, which can cause serious disabilities in speech, movement, and other basic activities, and can cause death. Having high blood pressure, especially in midlife, is linked to poorer cognitive function and dementia later in life.
complications_detailed.heart_valve_disease: High blood pressure can cause heart valve disease, which is when any valve in the heart is damaged or diseased.
complications_detailed.kidney_disease: Adults with diabetes, high blood pressure, or both have a higher risk of developing chronic kidney disease than those without these conditions.

lifestyle_management_detail: Get physical activity each week — about 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week.
Eat a healthy diet, including limiting sodium (salt) and alcohol.
In addition to lifestyle changes, some people with high blood pressure need to take medicine to manage it.
Talk with a health care team right away if you think you have high blood pressure, or if you've been told you have high blood pressure but do not have it under control.
By taking action to lower blood pressure, a person can help protect themselves against heart disease and stroke, also called cardiovascular disease (CVD).

pregnancy.overview: Some women have high blood pressure during pregnancy. This can put the mother and baby at risk for problems during the pregnancy. High blood pressure in pregnancy has become more common, but with good blood pressure control, mother and baby are more likely to stay healthy. Hypertensive disorders affect 5% to 10% of women during pregnancy, a 25% increase over the past two decades. High blood pressure is preventable and treatable, and getting treatment is important before, during, and after pregnancy.

complications.for_the_mother: Preeclampsia, eclampsia, stroke, the need for labor induction (giving medicine to start labor), and placental abruption (the placenta separating from the wall of the uterus).
complications.for_the_baby: Preterm delivery (birth before 37 weeks of pregnancy) and low birth weight (a baby born weighing less than 5 pounds, 8 ounces). When the mother's blood pressure is high, it is hard for the baby to get enough oxygen and nutrients to grow, which may cause the mother to deliver the baby early.

before_pregnancy: Make a plan for pregnancy and talk with a doctor or health care team about any health problems and any medicines being taken.
A doctor or health care team can help find medicines that are safe to take during pregnancy.
Discuss ways to keep a healthy weight through healthy eating and regular physical activity.
during_pregnancy: Get early and regular prenatal care, and go to every appointment with a doctor or health care professional.
Keep track of blood pressure at home with a home blood pressure monitor; contact a doctor if blood pressure is higher than usual or if there are symptoms of preeclampsia.
Talk to a doctor or insurance company about getting a home monitor.
Continue to choose healthy foods and keep a healthy weight.
after_pregnancy: Pay attention to how you feel after giving birth — having had high blood pressure during pregnancy means a higher risk for stroke and other problems after delivery.
Tell a doctor or call emergency services right away if symptoms of preeclampsia appear after delivery, since emergency medical care might be needed.

conditions_and_pregnancy.name: High blood pressure during pregnancy
conditions_and_pregnancy.definition: Occurs when a pregnant woman has a blood pressure reading of 140/90 mm Hg or higher in two readings that are 4 or more hours apart.

conditions_and_pregnancy.name: Severe high blood pressure during pregnancy
conditions_and_pregnancy.definition: Occurs when a pregnant woman has a blood pressure reading of 160/110 mm Hg on two or more occasions.

conditions_and_pregnancy.name: Chronic hypertension during pregnancy
conditions_and_pregnancy.definition: When a pregnant woman has pre-existing high blood pressure and is diagnosed in the first 20 weeks of pregnancy, or if the high blood pressure lasts 12 weeks after the woman has given birth.

conditions_and_pregnancy.name: Gestational hypertension
conditions_and_pregnancy.definition: When a pregnant woman who previously had normal blood pressure develops high blood pressure during pregnancy.

conditions_and_pregnancy.name: Preeclampsia
conditions_and_pregnancy.definition: Occurs when a woman who previously had normal blood pressure suddenly develops high blood pressure and protein is found in her urine, or she has other problems, after 20 weeks of pregnancy. Women who have chronic hypertension can also get preeclampsia.

conditions_and_pregnancy.name: Eclampsia
conditions_and_pregnancy.definition: A medical emergency. Eclampsia is when a pregnant woman with preeclampsia has seizures that have no other cause.

preeclampsia_and_eclampsia.overview: Preeclampsia is one of the leading causes of pregnancy-related death, occurring in about 2% to 8% of all pregnancies. Some women with preeclampsia can develop seizures — this is called eclampsia, which is a medical emergency. Health care professionals can recommend low-dose aspirin for some pregnant women at higher risk of preeclampsia; if taken at the appropriate time, low-dose aspirin has been shown to reduce the risk of preeclampsia.
symptoms: A headache that will not go away
Changes in vision, including blurry vision, seeing spots, or changes in eyesight
Pain in the upper stomach area
Swelling of the face or hands
preeclampsia_and_eclampsia.symptom_note: Some women have no symptoms of preeclampsia, which is why it's important to visit a health care team regularly, especially during pregnancy.
risk_factors: This is the first time giving birth
Had preeclampsia during a previous pregnancy
Has chronic (long-term) high blood pressure, chronic kidney disease, or both
Has a history of thrombophilia (a condition that increases risk of blood clots)
Pregnant with multiple babies (such as twins or triplets)
Became pregnant using in vitro fertilization
Has a family history of preeclampsia
Has type 1 or type 2 diabetes
Has obesity
Has lupus (an autoimmune disease)
Is older than 40
preeclampsia_and_eclampsia.postpartum_preeclampsia: In rare cases, preeclampsia can happen after giving birth. This is a serious medical condition known as postpartum preeclampsia, and it can happen in women without any history of preeclampsia during pregnancy. Symptoms are similar to preeclampsia and are typically diagnosed soon after delivery but can happen up to 6 weeks later.

risk_factors_detailed.overview: Risk factors that can increase the risk of high blood pressure include health conditions, lifestyle, and family history. Some risk factors cannot be controlled, such as age or family history, but steps can be taken to lower risk by changing the factors that can be controlled.
risk_factors_detailed.elevated_blood_pressure: Elevated blood pressure is blood pressure that is slightly higher than normal. High blood pressure usually develops over time, so having blood pressure that is slightly higher than normal increases the risk for developing chronic high blood pressure. A reading between 120/80 mm Hg and 129/80 mm Hg is considered elevated blood pressure.
conditions_that_increase_risk: Elevated blood pressure (a precursor stage that can progress to chronic hypertension if unmanaged)
other_factors_that_increase_risk: Family history — high blood pressure can run in families

conditions_that_increase_risk_detail.diabetes: About 6 out of 10 people who have diabetes also have high blood pressure. Diabetes causes sugars to build up in the blood and also increases the risk for heart disease. Talk with a doctor about ways to manage diabetes and control other risk factors.
conditions_that_increase_risk_detail.obesity: Having obesity is having excess body fat. Having obesity or overweight means the heart must work harder to pump blood and oxygen around the body, which over time can add stress to the heart and blood vessels. Obesity is linked to higher 'bad' cholesterol and triglyceride levels and to lower 'good' cholesterol levels. In addition to high blood pressure, having obesity can also lead to heart disease and diabetes.
conditions_that_increase_risk_detail.elevated_blood_pressure: Elevated blood pressure (120/80 mm Hg to 129/80 mm Hg) is slightly higher than normal and increases the risk of developing chronic high blood pressure over time.
conditions_that_increase_risk_detail.pregnancy: Some women develop high blood pressure during pregnancy, which can put mother and baby at risk for problems during or after the pregnancy. Anyone pregnant or planning to become pregnant should talk with their health care team about ways to stay safe.

behaviors_that_increase_risk_detail.overview: Lifestyle choices can increase the risk for high blood pressure. The good news is that healthy behaviors can lower that risk, and a doctor may recommend specific lifestyle changes to reduce it.
behaviors_that_increase_risk_detail.unhealthy_diet: A diet too high in sodium and too low in potassium puts a person at risk for high blood pressure. Eating too much sodium (an element in table salt) increases blood pressure, and most dietary sodium comes from processed and restaurant foods rather than the salt shaker. Not eating enough potassium — a mineral the body needs to work properly — can also increase blood pressure; foods high in potassium include bananas, potatoes, beans, and yogurt.
behaviors_that_increase_risk_detail.physical_inactivity: Getting regular physical activity helps the heart and blood vessels stay strong and healthy, which may help lower blood pressure. Regular activity can also help maintain a healthy weight, which may further help lower blood pressure.
behaviors_that_increase_risk_detail.too_much_alcohol: Drinking too much alcohol can raise blood pressure. Women should have no more than one drink a day, and men should have no more than two drinks a day.
behaviors_that_increase_risk_detail.tobacco_use: Tobacco use increases the risk for high blood pressure. Smoking can damage the heart and blood vessels: nicotine raises blood pressure, and breathing in carbon monoxide (produced from smoking tobacco) reduces the amount of oxygen the blood can carry.

other_factors_that_increase_risk_detail.family_and_environment: Family members share genes, behaviors, lifestyles, and environments that can influence their health and their risk for disease. High blood pressure can run in a family, and risk can also increase based on age and race or ethnicity.
other_factors_that_increase_risk_detail.genetics_and_family_history: Heredity is the process by which family members pass traits from one generation to another through genes. Genes likely play some role in high blood pressure, heart disease, and other related conditions; however, it's also likely that people with a family history of high blood pressure share common environments and other potential factors that increase their risk. Risk can increase even more when heredity combines with unhealthy lifestyle choices such as smoking and eating an unhealthy diet. Family health history — a record of the diseases and health conditions people in a family have had — is a useful tool for understanding health risks and preventing disease.

other_characteristics.age: Because blood pressure tends to rise with age, the risk for high blood pressure increases with age. About 9 out of 10 Americans will develop high blood pressure during their lifetime.
other_characteristics.sex: Both men and women can have high blood pressure. Women are about as likely as men to develop high blood pressure at some point during their lives.
other_characteristics.race_or_ethnicity: Black people develop high blood pressure more often than white people, Hispanics, Asians, Pacific Islanders, American Indians, or Alaska Natives do. Compared with White people, Black people also tend to develop high blood pressure earlier in life.

prevention_detailed.overview: Practicing healthy living habits can help prevent high blood pressure. Key steps include talking with a health care team about eating a variety of foods rich in potassium, fiber, and protein and lower in salt (sodium) and saturated fat; reaching and keeping a healthy weight through healthy food choices and regular physical activity; and stopping smoking or reducing alcohol consumption.
prevention_detailed.eat_a_healthy_diet: Choosing healthy meal and snack options — including plenty of fresh fruits and vegetables — helps avoid high blood pressure and its complications. The DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) eating plan is a healthy diet plan with a proven record of helping people lower their blood pressure.
prevention_detailed.keep_a_healthy_weight: Having overweight or obesity increases the risk for high blood pressure. Talking with a health care team about ways to reach a healthy weight — including choosing healthy foods and getting regular physical activity — can help.
prevention_detailed.get_regular_physical_activity: Adults should get at least 150 minutes (2 hours and 30 minutes) of moderate-intensity exercise, such as brisk walking or bicycling, every week — about 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week. Children and adolescents should get 1 hour of physical activity every day.
prevention_detailed.do_not_smoke: Smoking raises blood pressure and increases the risk for heart attack and stroke. Not starting is best; for those who already smoke, quitting will lower the risk for heart disease.
prevention_detailed.limit_alcohol: Drinking too much alcohol can raise blood pressure. Men should have no more than 2 alcoholic drinks per day, and women should have no more than 1 alcoholic drink per day.
prevention_detailed.get_enough_sleep: Getting enough sleep is important to overall health and helps keep the heart and blood vessels healthy. Not getting enough sleep on a regular basis is linked to an increased risk of heart disease, high blood pressure, and stroke.

managing.overview: Measuring blood pressure is an important step toward controlling high blood pressure. Making healthy lifestyle choices — such as getting regular physical activity and not smoking — can help keep blood pressure levels healthy. It's important to work with a health care team to manage high blood pressure and related conditions.
managing.measuring_regularly: Measuring blood pressure is an important step toward keeping a healthy blood pressure, since high blood pressure often has no symptoms — checking blood pressure is the only way to know for sure whether it's too high. Anyone who learns they have high blood pressure should take steps to control it, which lowers the risk for heart disease and stroke. Anyone pregnant or planning to become pregnant who has high blood pressure should talk with their health care team about ways to keep themselves and their baby safe.

managing_related_health_conditions.diabetes: Most people with diabetes — about 6 out of 10 — also have high blood pressure. A health care professional may recommend testing if there are symptoms of diabetes. Sticking to a diabetes treatment plan — taking medicines as prescribed, eating well, and getting regular physical activity, and keeping blood sugar (glucose) within the target range set by a doctor — can also help reduce the risk for high blood pressure.
managing_related_health_conditions.obesity: Having overweight or obesity means the heart must work harder to pump blood and oxygen around the body. Staying at a healthy weight reduces the stress on the heart and reduces the risk for heart disease, heart attack, and stroke.
managing_related_health_conditions.mental_health: People who have depression, anxiety, stress, or post-traumatic stress disorder over a long period of time may develop other health problems, including an increased heart rate and high blood pressure. It's important to recognize the signs and symptoms of mental health disorders and heart disease, and to talk with a health care team about potential heart conditions in relation to mental health.

lifestyle_changes: Get regular physical activity — staying physically active is one of the best things a person can do for their health; it helps keep the heart and blood vessels strong and can help maintain a healthy weight.
Do not smoke — smoking damages blood vessels and greatly increases the risk of high blood pressure, heart disease, heart attack, and stroke.
Eat healthy foods — choosing healthy meal and snack options, with plenty of fresh fruits and vegetables, can help avoid high blood pressure and its complications.
Keep a healthy weight — staying at a healthy weight reduces the stress on the heart and lowers the risk for heart disease, heart attack, and stroke.
managing.creating_a_care_plan: A person and their health care team can work together to create a care plan for high blood pressure and other conditions that can lead to it. It helps to discuss the treatment plan regularly and bring a list of questions to appointments.

medication.overview: Many people need to take medicine in addition to making lifestyle changes to help keep their blood pressure at healthy levels. A health care team may prescribe one of several kinds of blood pressure medicine, and some people need more than one type to control their blood pressure.
medicine_classes: (and other classes — for the latest information on each type, see the U.S. FDA's high blood pressure webpage)
how_they_work: Causing the body to get rid of water, which decreases the amount of water and salt in the body to a healthy level (diuretics)
Making the heart beat with less force
Blocking nerve activity that can restrict blood vessels
medication.how_to_know_if_medicine_is_needed: A health care team will advise whether medicine for high blood pressure is needed, based on blood pressure readings over a period of time. Anyone using a home blood pressure monitor should record or write down their readings to share with their care team.
medication.benefits_and_risks: Blood pressure medicines can help keep blood pressure at healthy levels and therefore greatly reduce the risk of heart disease, heart attack, and stroke. All medicines carry some risk, so it's worth discussing the best blood pressure medicine choice, its benefits, risks, and side effects, and any other health problems, with a doctor.
medication.side_effects: Most of the time, blood pressure medicines do not cause side effects. Some people have mild side effects, including dizziness, headaches, swelling in the legs or feet, or stomach problems. Some over-the-counter medicines, such as nasal decongestants, can also raise blood pressure and interact with blood pressure medicines — so it's important to tell a doctor about any other medicines or supplements being taken.
medication.adherence_note: It is important to take blood pressure medicine exactly as a doctor prescribes it. Do not stop taking a current medicine without talking to a doctor or pharmacist first — stopping blood pressure medicine without first talking to a health care team could lead to serious health consequences.

asthma.name: Asthma
asthma.source: World Health Organization — Asthma fact sheet
key_facts: Asthma is a major noncommunicable disease and the most common chronic disease among children.
It affected an estimated 363 million people in 2023 and caused 442,000 deaths.
Inhaled medication can control symptoms well and allow people with asthma to lead a normal, active life.
Most asthma-related deaths occur in low- and lower-middle-income countries, largely due to under-diagnosis and under-treatment.
asthma.overview: Asthma is a chronic lung condition caused by inflammation and tightening of the muscles around the airways, making it harder to breathe. Symptoms can be mild or severe and tend to come and go over time, sometimes flaring into a more serious episode known as an asthma attack.
symptoms: Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing, sometimes even at rest
risk_factors: Family history of asthma
Other allergic conditions such as eczema or hay fever
Low birth weight or premature birth
Early exposure to tobacco smoke or air pollution
Childhood respiratory infections
Being overweight or obese
severe_warning_signs: Breathlessness that keeps worsening or doesn't improve with a reliever inhaler
Difficulty speaking full sentences due to breathlessness
Bluish tint to lips or face
Breathlessness severe enough to interfere with normal activity or sleep
asthma.escalation_note: A severe asthma attack that doesn't respond to the usual reliever inhaler is a medical emergency and needs urgent care — in the most severe cases, asthma attacks can be fatal without prompt treatment.
prevention: Identify and avoid personal asthma triggers
Reduce exposure to tobacco smoke and air pollution
Manage related allergic conditions
Follow an asthma action plan developed with a healthcare provider
asthma.treatment: Asthma has no cure but is well controlled with inhaled medication: bronchodilators to open the airways during symptoms, steroid inhalers to reduce underlying inflammation, and combination inhalers containing both. A spacer device can make inhalers easier and more effective to use, particularly for children.
additional_sources: U.S. CDC — About Asthma
U.S. CDC — Controlling Asthma
U.S. CDC — What to Do When an Emergency Occurs (Asthma)
U.S. CDC — Living with Asthma
U.S. CDC — Respiratory Infections and Asthma
Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America (AAFA) — Asthma Facts and Figures
cdc_key_points: Asthma is a disease that affects your lungs.
It is one of the most common long-term diseases of children, but adults can have asthma, too.
Asthma causes wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and coughing at night or early in the morning.
You can control your asthma by knowing the warning signs of an asthma attack, staying away from things that cause an attack, and following your doctor's advice.
asthma.cdc_diagnosis: It can be hard to tell if someone has asthma, especially in children under age 5. During a checkup, a doctor may ask if you cough a lot, especially at night, whether breathing problems are worse after physical activity or at certain times of year, about chest tightness, wheezing, and colds lasting more than 10 days, and whether anyone in your family has or has had asthma, allergies, or other breathing problems. The doctor may also do a breathing test called spirometry, which tests how much air you breathe out after taking a very deep breath, before and after you use asthma medicine.
asthma.cdc_symptom_management: Take your medicine exactly as your doctor tells you and stay away from things that can trigger an attack to control your asthma. Everyone with asthma does not take the same medicine — some medicines are inhaled and others taken as a pill. Asthma medicines can be used as reliever therapy or controller therapy. If you need to use your reliever medicine more and more, visit your doctor to see if you need a different medicine. Controller medicines help you have fewer and milder asthma attacks. Asthma medicines can have side effects, but most side effects are mild and soon go away — ask your doctor about the side effects of your medicines.

cdc_common_triggers.secondhand_smoke: Smoke created by a smoker and breathed in by a second person can trigger an asthma attack. If you have asthma, people should never smoke near you.
cdc_common_triggers.dust_mites: Dust mites are microscopic bugs found in many homes that can trigger an asthma attack. To prevent attacks: use allergen-proof mattress and pillowcase covers; don't use down-filled pillows, quilts, or comforters; wash bedding weekly and dry it completely; vacuum regularly using a vacuum equipped with a HEPA filter; and keep relative humidity levels in the home low, around 30-50%.
cdc_common_triggers.air_pollution: Air pollution can trigger an asthma attack. This pollution can come from factories, cars, or wildfire smoke. Pay attention to air quality forecasts on radio, television, and the internet.
cdc_common_triggers.cockroaches_and_pests: Cockroaches and other pests are often found where food is eaten and crumbs are left behind. To control pests: remove as many water and food sources as you can; clean dishes, crumbs, and spills right away; store food in airtight containers; keep trash in a closed container; vacuum or sweep areas that might attract cockroaches or mice often; seal cracks in cabinets, walls, baseboards, and around plumbing; and avoid using sprays and foggers, as these can cause asthma attacks.
cdc_common_triggers.furry_pets: Furry pets can trigger an asthma attack if you are allergic to them. If you can't or don't want to find a new home for the pet, protect yourself by keeping pets out of bedrooms, washing furry pets, using an air cleaner with a HEPA filter, and using allergen-proof mattress and pillow covers. Note: people with asthma are not allergic to their pet's fur, so trimming a pet's fur will not help asthma.
cdc_common_triggers.mold: Breathing in mold can trigger an asthma attack whether or not you are allergic to mold. Indoors, mold grows in damp areas such as kitchens, bathrooms, and basements, or where water damage has occurred. To reduce mold exposure: dry damp or wet items within 24 to 48 hours; fix water leaks as soon as you can; replace ceiling tiles and carpet if they are moldy; use an air conditioner or dehumidifier to keep indoor humidity low; keep humidity under 50% and check more than once a day with a hygrometer; scrub mold off hard surfaces with detergent and water and dry completely; and run the bathroom exhaust fan or open the window when showering.
other_triggers: Infections linked to flu, colds, and RSV
Breathing in some chemicals or fragrances
Bad weather, such as thunderstorms or high humidity and cold, dry air
Some foods and medicines for people allergic to them
Physical exercise or strong emotions that lead to very fast breathing

cdc_emergency_guidance.first_steps: Follow your Asthma Action Plan: take all your asthma medication exactly as prescribed and don't stop any medications or change your treatment plan without talking to your healthcare provider; make sure you have at least 30 days of non-prescription medications and supplies in case you need to stay home for a long time; know how to use your inhaler; and avoid your asthma triggers.
cdc_emergency_guidance.everyday_precautions: Wash your hands with soap and water — the best way to reduce germs — before, during, and after preparing food; before eating food; after using the toilet; after changing diapers or cleaning up a child who has used the toilet; before and after caring for someone who is sick; after blowing your nose, coughing, or sneezing; and after touching garbage. If soap and water are not available, use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol.
cdc_emergency_guidance.clean_and_disinfect: Clean things you or your family touch frequently, like tables, doorknobs, light switches, countertops, handles, desks, phones, remotes, keyboards, toilets, faucets, and sinks. Avoid disinfectants that can cause an asthma attack — have someone who doesn't have asthma clean and disinfect when possible. When using cleaning and disinfecting products: make sure people with asthma are not in the room; avoid products that can cause an asthma attack; open windows or doors and use a fan that blows air outdoors; apply the cleaner to a cloth or paper towel rather than spraying it into the air; and always follow the instructions on the product label.

cdc_asthma_action_plan.overview: Everyone with asthma needs their own Asthma Action Plan. Work with your health care provider to create a plan that works for you — the goal is to prevent and control your asthma attacks. CDC provides a downloadable, fillable PDF Asthma Action Plan Tool.
cdc_asthma_action_plan.green_zone_doing_well: I don't have cough, wheezing, chest tightness, or trouble breathing at any time. I can do all the things I usually do. When I use a peak flow meter, my peak flow is more than 80 percent of my best peak flow. Continue taking your daily controller medicine.
cdc_asthma_action_plan.yellow_zone_getting_worse: I have some cough, wheezing, chest tightness, or trouble breathing. Or I wake up at night because of my asthma. Or I can't do some of the things I usually do. Or when I use a peak flow meter, my peak flow is half to about three quarters of my best peak flow. Add your reliever medicine and continue your daily controller medicine. If your symptoms get better after an hour, keep checking them and continue your daily controller medicine.
cdc_asthma_action_plan.red_zone_medical_alert: I have a lot of trouble breathing — this zone signals a medical alert requiring urgent action.

asthma.cdc_respiratory_infections_note: Respiratory infections like influenza (flu), COVID-19, and RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus) can be more serious for individuals with asthma because they can lead to pneumonia and asthma attacks. Get vaccinated for respiratory diseases when vaccines are available and your provider says you can.
asthma.cdc_flu_and_asthma: People with asthma are more likely to have serious health problems from getting the flu. Flu virus infection can cause an asthma attack. An annual flu vaccine is the most important step to protect yourself and others from flu; the flu vaccine may be given at the same time as other vaccines.
asthma.cdc_covid19_and_asthma: COVID-19 infection can cause an asthma attack in people with asthma. Staying up to date on COVID-19 vaccines is the most important thing to protect yourself; the vaccine may be given at the same time as other vaccines. People with moderate to severe asthma, particularly if not well-controlled, might be at higher risk of getting very sick from COVID-19.
asthma.cdc_rsv_and_asthma: RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus) is a common virus that usually causes mild, cold-like symptoms. Most people recover in a week or two, but RSV can be serious, especially for infants and older adults. If you have asthma, an RSV infection can cause an asthma attack. RSV vaccines are available for some people.
cdc_protecting_against_respiratory_disea: Get vaccinated when vaccines are available for a respiratory disease.
Wash your hands often with soap and water for at least 20 seconds; use alcohol-based hand sanitizer if soap and water aren't available.
Keep your hands off your face — avoid touching your eyes, nose, and mouth with unwashed hands.
Avoid close contact with sick people, such as kissing and sharing cups or eating utensils with people who have cold-like symptoms.
Clean and disinfect surfaces and objects frequently touched, such as toys, doorknobs, and mobile devices.
Wear a NIOSH-approved N95 respirator or other mask in crowded indoor spaces.
Improve ventilation and filtration to help prevent virus particles from spreading.
cdc_other_steps_to_stay_healthy: Always follow your Asthma Action Plan.
Continue current medications, including any inhalers with steroids (corticosteroids) in them. Know how to use your inhaler.
Do not stop any medications or change your asthma treatment plan without talking to your healthcare provider.
Talk to your healthcare provider, insurer, and pharmacist about creating an emergency supply of prescription medications, such as asthma inhalers.
Make sure you have 30 days of non-prescription medications and supplies on hand in case you need to stay home for a long time.
Be careful around cleaning agents and disinfectants, since some can cause asthma attacks or other adverse reactions.
asthma.cdc_protect_others: Protect others by staying home when you are sick (from work, school, and public areas) and wearing a mask or NIOSH-approved N95 respirator with the best fit and protection when around others.
asthma.what_is_asthma_detail: Asthma is a chronic (long-term) disease that causes inflammation and swelling of the airways. In lungs with asthma, the small muscles around the airways squeeze and tighten, the inside of the airways swell, and extra mucus clogs the airways. There is no cure for asthma, but asthma attacks can be prevented and treated to help people have better quality of life. Asthma can be managed and controlled, but without appropriate treatment it can cause permanent lung damage, reduced lung function, and death.
uncontrolled_asthma_can_cause: Reduced quality of life and physical ability
asthma.symptom_detail: Asthma symptoms include trouble breathing (shortness of breath, shallow breathing, or fast breathing), wheezing, coughing, and tightness or pain in the chest. Common signs and symptoms of asthma include shortness of breath, cough, chest tightness or pain, wheeze (a whistling sound when breathing), and waking at night.
asthma_emergency_signs_detailed: Trouble breathing that makes it hard to talk or walk
Color changes on skin, lips, tongue, or fingertips from not getting enough air
Chest sucks in between neck, chest plate, or ribs when breathing in
Fingertips, nails, or area around mouth changing color (grayish, whitish, or bluish)

us_prevalence_statistics.source_note: Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America (AAFA) — Asthma Facts and Figures
us_prevalence_statistics.overall: Nearly 28 million people in the U.S. have asthma. This equals about 8% (8 out of 100) people.

adults.overview: About 23 million U.S. adults (or about 9 out of 100) ages 18 and older have asthma.

by_race_ethnicity.overview: Asthma rates are highest in Black and Indigenous adults in the U.S.
by_race_ethnicity.black_adults: About 3 million Black adults (or about 10 out of 100) have asthma.
by_race_ethnicity.indigenous_adults: About 347,000 Indigenous adults (or about 10 out of 100) have asthma.
by_race_ethnicity.white_adults: About 18 million White adults (or about 9 out of 100) have asthma.
by_race_ethnicity.hispanic_adults: About 3 million Hispanic adults (or about 7 out of 100) have asthma.
by_race_ethnicity.asian_adults: About 823,000 Asian adults (or about 5 out of 100) have asthma.

adults.by_sex: Asthma is more common in female adults than male adults. Around 11% (11 out of 100) of female adults have asthma.
adults.by_income: Asthma is more common in adults living below the federal poverty level than adults with higher incomes. About 12 out of 100 adults living below the federal poverty level ($15,060 in 2024) have asthma, compared to about 8 out of 100 adults who made $30,120 or more in 2024.

by_sexual_orientation.overview: Asthma is more common in gay and bisexual adults compared to straight adults.
by_sexual_orientation.men: A 2022 report found that 11 out of 100 straight men had asthma, compared to 13 out of 100 gay men and 15 out of 100 bisexual men.
by_sexual_orientation.women: The same report found that 14 out of 100 straight women had asthma, compared to 21 out of 100 lesbian women and 24 out of 100 bisexual women.

children.overview: There are close to 5 million U.S. children (or about 7 out of 100) under the age of 18 with asthma.
children.chronic_disease_ranking: Asthma is a top chronic disease in U.S. children. Only tooth decay (cavities) is more common than asthma.
children.long_covid_note: Long COVID affects 4% (or 4 out of 100) of children with asthma, which equals about 3 million children.
children.by_race: Black children are nearly 2 times more likely to have asthma compared to White children. About 1 million (or 11 out of 100) Black children have asthma.

anemia.name: Anemia
anemia.source: World Health Organization — Anaemia fact sheet
key_facts: Anaemia mainly affects young children, pregnant and postpartum women, and menstruating adolescent girls and women.
Globally, an estimated 40% of children aged 6–59 months, 37% of pregnant women, and 30% of women aged 15–49 are affected.
Low- and lower-middle-income countries, and rural or poorer populations, bear the greatest burden.
Anaemia is both preventable and treatable.
anemia.overview: Anaemia occurs when the number of red blood cells, or the haemoglobin within them, is lower than normal — meaning less oxygen reaches the body's organs and tissues. It is considered a symptom of an underlying issue rather than a standalone disease, and can result from nutrient deficiencies, infections, chronic conditions, blood loss, or inherited blood disorders.
symptoms: Shortness of breath, especially with exertion
severe_warning_signs: Pale mucous membranes, skin, or nail beds
Rapid breathing or rapid heart rate
anemia.escalation_note: Severe anaemia, especially in pregnant women or young children, can affect development and pregnancy outcomes and should be evaluated by a healthcare provider promptly rather than managed with diet changes alone.
causes: Iron, vitamin A, folate, B12, or riboflavin deficiency
Infections such as malaria, TB, HIV, or parasitic infections
Heavy menstrual bleeding or blood loss during childbirth
Inherited red blood cell disorders such as thalassaemia or sickle cell disease
prevention: Eat a varied diet rich in iron — lean meats, fish, poultry, legumes, fortified cereals, and leafy greens
Pair iron-rich foods with vitamin C sources to improve absorption
Avoid tea, coffee, or calcium close to iron-rich meals, as they reduce absorption
Prevent and treat underlying infections such as malaria or parasitic worms
See a doctor for heavy menstrual bleeding, who may recommend supplements or other treatment
Take iron or other supplements only if recommended by a qualified healthcare provider
anemia.treatment: Treatment depends on the underlying cause and can include dietary changes, supplements prescribed by a health professional, treating an underlying infection, or managing heavy blood loss. Inherited blood disorders such as sickle cell disease or thalassaemia require specific, ongoing medical management.
additional_sources: Peer-reviewed literature review on anemia etiology, pathophysiology, impact, and prevention (PMC, NCBI — search method covered Scopus, PubMed, ProQuest, Google Scholar, and ScienceDirect; articles from 2012–2023)

who_hemoglobin_thresholds.note: Hemoglobin concentration (g/dL) thresholds used by WHO to classify anemia severity, which vary by age, sex, and pregnancy status.

types_by_morphology.overview: Anemia can be classified by red blood cell size, shape, and color (morphology), which helps point toward the underlying cause. Healthy red blood cells are biconcave and red in color, with an average volume of 80–100 femtoliters (fL), a surface area of around 135±15 mm², a diameter of around 7.8 mm, and a thickness of around 0.81 mm.

types.cause: Damage to the bone marrow, which impairs its ability to produce red blood cells.

Lack of iron (a lack of heme synthesis). Red blood cells are smaller than usual (low MCV) and paler than usual (hypochromic, low MCHC). Also seen with sideroblastic conditions, chronic blood loss, or impaired globin synthesis such as thalassemia.
Chronic disease, a disorder in red blood cell production in the bone marrow, kidney failure, or bleeding.
Damage to red blood cells before they reach maturity.

Deficiencies in vitamin B12 or folic acid, or protein-synthesis and autoimmune disorders. Red blood cells are larger than usual, with normal hemoglobin concentration (normochromic; increased MCV, normal MCHC), caused by interference with or cessation of DNA nucleic-acid synthesis.
Genetic disturbances that cause red blood cells to form abnormal shapes, as seen in sickle cell disease and thalassemia.

types_by_morphology.biological_mechanism: On a biological level, anemia develops from an imbalance between red blood cell (erythrocyte) loss and production. This can result from ineffective or deficient erythropoiesis (red blood cell formation) and/or excessive erythrocyte loss due to hemolysis, blood loss, or both. Anemia is often classified by this underlying biological mechanism — for example, iron deficiency anemia (IDA), hemolytic anemia, and inflammatory anemia (AI). In some cases, such as obese teenagers, anemia can occur due to a lack of proper nutritional intake of iron, folate, and vitamin B12, which affects red blood cell production.

causes_direct_and_indirect.overview: Anemia results from direct causes, such as nutrient deficiencies and chronic blood loss, and indirect (distal) causes, such as socioeconomic factors and limited healthcare access, which influence dietary habits and overall health and increase anemia risk.
direct_causes: Genetic abnormalities (e.g. sickle cell disease, thalassemia)
Bleeding as a consequence of an accident
causes_direct_and_indirect.socioeconomic_note: Many determinants are interrelated. Poverty is a significant determinant of health and nutrition, and poor socioeconomic position is associated with a greater risk of anemia in women and children. Low levels of education are also associated with a greater risk of anemia. A recent analysis of 53 demographic and health surveys with hemoglobin data found that anemia among preschool children (affecting 70% of the population studied in that analysis) was strongly associated with maternal anemia, household wealth, maternal education, and low birth weight.
causes_direct_and_indirect.iron_deficiency_detail: The most common cause of anemia is a lack of iron. This can result from insufficient iron absorption, an increased need for iron, or increased iron loss — such as during menstruation. Chronic blood loss from digestive disorders (ulcers, NSAID use, cancers, diverticulitis, hemorrhoids, and hookworms), menstrual bleeding, urinary tract bleeding, or respiratory tract bleeding can all cause iron deficiency. Increased iron needs occur in premature infants, during growth, and in pregnancy. Absorption issues, such as those following gastrectomy, or from tropical disease or chronic colitis, can also contribute.
causes_direct_and_indirect.iron_function_note: Iron bound to protein forms hemoglobin, which transports oxygen throughout the body. Iron is an essential micronutrient that plays a role in various cellular metabolic processes, including energy production, enzyme synthesis, maintenance of neuronal activity, and support of the immune system.

pathophysiology_detailed.overview: Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) occurs when the body's need for iron exceeds the available supply, so the amount of iron is insufficient for optimal hemoglobin formation. This condition causes the red blood cells formed to have a smaller size (microcytic) and a paler color (hypochromic).

stages.description: Depletion of iron levels in the bone marrow, or a decrease in iron reserves, characterized by low ferritin concentrations.

A reduced erythropoiesis process, resulting in decreased red blood cell production. This occurs when iron reserves are depleted, the supply of iron to erythrocyte-forming cells is reduced, and transferrin saturation decreases — even though hemoglobin levels are still within the normal range.

Iron stores have been fully depleted, and hematocrit and hemoglobin levels decrease. The red blood cells formed in this stage are smaller than usual (microcytic) and have a low hemoglobin concentration (hypochromic).

impact_on_adolescents.prevalence_note: The prevalence of anemia in women often rises at puberty due to menstruation and is commonly seen in young women aged 10–19 years, a transition period marked by changes in physique and psyche. Some studies report that as many as 78.5% of teenage girls suffer from anemia, while other research indicates around 70% of teenagers and adolescent girls are affected — reflecting poor nutritional status and health.
impact_on_adolescents.general_impact: Anemia can lower the body's resistance so that teenagers become more susceptible to illness, and can cause a decline in activities and academic achievement because of reduced concentration.
impact_on_adolescents.pregnancy_impact: Iron deficiency, combined with generally poor nutritional status, can be harmful during a later pregnancy — increasing the risk of babies born with low birth weight, and even the risk of death in mothers and babies.
impact_on_adolescents.cognitive_and_school_impact: Anemia is associated with a decline in cognition, learning, and school performance in children, and can affect concentration, educational success, productivity, and physical capacity in teenage girls, as well as increasing the risk of infection.
impact_on_adolescents.cognitive_mechanism: Teenage girls are especially vulnerable to anemia because of the need for increased iron to support rapid mental growth and development, as well as to replace iron lost through menstruation. A lack of iron can cause cognitive disturbance in humans, with damage to the mitochondria of the brain thought to underlie this change. Iron-deficiency-related cognitive impairment is linked to attention, intelligence, and sensory perception, as well as to emotions and behavior. Juvenile anemia has also been reported to increase the risk of psychiatric disorders, including mood disorders, autism spectrum disorders, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and other developmental disorders.
impact_on_adolescents.maternal_perinatal_impact: An anemic teenager contributes to a higher risk of maternal mortality and an increased incidence of low birth weight, perinatal death, and fetal death. Adolescent childbirth can impair growth due to malnutrition, and early pregnancy and breastfeeding deplete micronutrients like iron, increasing the risk of anemia; poor nutrition during pregnancy can further worsen the condition.
impact_on_adolescents.intergenerational_cycle: Teenage girls who are frail and become pregnant tend to give birth to babies with low body weight. Anemia during adolescence can progress into pregnancy, raising the risk of premature or low-birth-weight (LBW) babies. LBW babies can grow up stunted, and may go on to become malnourished teenage girls and pregnant women themselves, potentially giving birth to the next stunted generation — children who are not only short but may also have lower intelligence (IQ), psychological disorders, and an increased risk of diabetes, hypertension, and various other chronic diseases later in life.

prevention_detailed.overview: Efforts to prevent anemia require a comprehensive approach addressing multiple contributing factors, generally grouped into three main areas: improving dietary intake, enhancing educational awareness, and promoting behavior modification. Efforts to prevent and control anemia in adolescents are typically carried out through three main programs: iron supplementation, nutrition education, and food fortification. Involving teenagers as role models for their peers is also considered valuable for promoting healthy lifestyles among the teenage generation, and prevention methods are more effective when adapted to be fun and engaging for teenagers.
through_food_intake: Fortification of food to increase nutritional content
Supplementation with iron and folic acid
Fortification to improve overall micronutrient status
through_education: Nutrition education to improve knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding anemia
prevention_detailed.dietary_detail: Taking food supplements rich in vitamins and minerals is one measure to prevent anemia. Folate can be consumed from green leafy vegetables, citrus fruits, and animal protein; folic acid is metabolized into tetrafolic acid, which is needed to synthesize the iron-containing nucleic acids obtained from meat — the iron complex is absorbed in the duodenum and jejunum and then stored, largely in the form of ferritin. Supplementation, fortification, and dietary diversification programs are key steps in anemia prevention. Some governments also provide deworming medication, and treat concurrent disease alongside folate/iron supplementation through blood-enhancement tablets.

compliance_challenges.overview: Implementation of programs providing iron/blood supplement tablets to teenagers still faces obstacles, particularly low compliance.
compliance_challenges.data: 2018 Riskesdas data (Indonesia) shows that only about 32% of teenagers comply with taking blood supplement tablets, while the other 68% did not follow through with consumption.
compliance_challenges.improving_compliance: Necessary steps to improve compliance include health-based education, such as peer education, delivered in coordination with school health programs/enterprises.

research_advances.overview: Anemia research is advancing on several fronts, including new treatments, improved understanding of pathophysiology, earlier detection, and better nutritional interventions.
research_advances.new_treatments: Research is focusing on new treatments such as gene therapy and drugs that boost erythropoietin (EPO) and red blood cell production, offering new hope for patients with chronic anemia, such as that caused by kidney disease. There are also efforts to create iron supplements that are easier for the body to absorb and more effective in treating iron deficiency anemia, which could increase iron absorption from both food and supplements.
research_advances.pathophysiology_research: Advances in genomics and proteomics are providing breakthroughs in understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying anemia associated with chronic diseases such as cancer and colitis. Understanding the cellular signaling pathways and transcription factors involved may allow more targeted therapies to be developed.
research_advances.detection_and_screening: Early detection and screening for anemia is a priority area of research. New DNA-based diagnostic methods and biomarkers are being developed to detect anemia more accurately and efficiently, alongside efforts to create portable and affordable screening tools for areas with limited resources.
research_advances.nutrition_and_fortification_research: Nutritional interventions and food fortification have also received significant research attention. Field studies are underway to test the effectiveness and safety of various strategies for enriching foods with iron, folic acid, and vitamin B12 to prevent anemia, and researchers are working to develop more effective and culturally acceptable nutritional supplements for at-risk populations.

prevalence_data_points.global_2021: According to the 2021 Global Nutrition Report, an estimated 570.8 million children, girls, and women of reproductive age suffer from anemia.
prevalence_data_points.trend_concern: Rather than progressing toward lower prevalence, an increase in anemia prevalence observed over recent years is projected, by 2025, to result in prevalence more than double the originally agreed global target rate (an estimated 31.2% versus a 14.3% target).
prevalence_data_points.indonesia_2018: According to 2018 Riskesdas data (Indonesia), national anemia prevalence was 48.9%, with the proportion of anemia among women at 27.2%.
prevalence_data_points.adolescent_prevalence_estimates: Estimates of anemia prevalence specifically among teenage girls vary by study, ranging from around 70% to as high as 78.5% in some research.

yellow_fever.name: Yellow Fever
yellow_fever.source: World Health Organization — Yellow fever fact sheet
key_facts: Yellow fever is a mosquito-borne viral disease, spread mainly by day-biting mosquitoes.
27 African countries and 13 Latin American countries are classified as high-risk for outbreaks.
A single dose of vaccine provides lifelong protection.
An estimated 67,000–173,000 severe infections and 31,000–82,000 deaths occur each year, with most of the burden in Africa.
yellow_fever.overview: Yellow fever is a vaccine-preventable, epidemic-prone viral disease with an incubation period of 3–6 days. Most infections cause a short, mild illness, but a portion of cases progress to a severe, life-threatening second phase.
yellow_fever.symptom_onset: Initial symptoms typically resolve within 3–4 days. However, about 15% of infected people go on to develop severe disease, marked by a return of high fever, jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes), vomiting, bleeding from the mouth, nose, eyes, or stomach, and organ failure — roughly half of people who reach this severe stage die within 7–10 days.
yellow_fever.escalation_note: A returning high fever with jaundice, bleeding, or reduced urine output after initial improvement is a medical emergency and needs immediate hospital care.
prevention: Get vaccinated — a single dose gives lifelong immunity for most people
Avoid mosquito bites through repellents and protective clothing
Eliminate standing water where mosquitoes breed
Note that bed nets are less effective here since these mosquitoes bite mainly during the day
yellow_fever.vaccine_notes: Vaccination is not recommended for infants under 9 months, pregnant women (except during active outbreaks), people with severe egg allergies, or those with severe immunodeficiency. People over 60 should discuss the risk–benefit of vaccination with a doctor.
yellow_fever.treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment in routine use. Care is supportive — rest, hydration, and management of fever and organ complications. Jaundice signals severe disease and usually requires hospitalization, often in intensive care.

stroke.name: Stroke
stroke.source: World Health Organization — Stroke fact sheet
key_facts: Stroke was the third leading cause of death and disability globally in 2021, with an estimated 93.8 million existing cases.
There were 11.9 million new stroke cases in 2021.
The lifetime risk of stroke has risen 50% over the past 20 years — 1 in 4 adults is now predicted to experience a stroke in their lifetime.
Most of the global stroke burden is linked to modifiable risk factors, especially high blood pressure.
stroke.overview: A stroke is a medical emergency that happens when blood flow to part of the brain is interrupted, either by a blockage (ischaemic stroke) or bleeding (haemorrhagic stroke), leading to brain cell damage. A transient ischaemic attack (TIA) causes similar symptoms for a few minutes without lasting damage, but is a serious warning sign that a full stroke may follow.
symptoms: Sudden dizziness, loss of balance, or loss of coordination
Sudden weakness in one or both arms
stroke.escalation_note: Any of these symptoms appearing suddenly is a medical emergency — call for emergency help immediately. Treatment within hours of symptom onset significantly improves the chances of recovery.

modifiable: High blood pressure (the single leading contributor, raising risk nearly threefold)
Diet high in sodium and low in fruits/vegetables
non_modifiable: Pre-existing heart conditions such as atrial fibrillation or heart failure

prevention: Control blood pressure through lifestyle and, where needed, medication
Reduce or stop tobacco use
Eat a balanced diet with plenty of fruit and vegetables, and less salt, saturated fat, and sugar
Get at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise per week
Manage related conditions such as diabetes and irregular heart rhythms
Limit alcohol use
stroke.treatment: Stroke requires emergency brain imaging (CT or MRI) as soon as possible. Ischaemic stroke may be treated with clot-dissolving medication given within hours of symptom onset, sometimes alongside a procedure to physically remove the clot. Haemorrhagic stroke is managed with blood pressure control, specialist intensive care, and sometimes surgery. Rehabilitation — physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and speech therapy — plays a major role in recovery afterward.
additional_sources: U.S. CDC — Stroke Facts
U.S. CDC — About Stroke
U.S. CDC — About Women and Stroke
U.S. CDC — About Men and Stroke
cdc_key_points: Stroke risk increases with age, but strokes can — and do — occur at any age.
Early action is important for stroke; the chances of survival are greater when emergency treatment begins quickly.
Stroke statistics vary by race and ethnicity.
Stroke causes parts of the brain to become damaged or die; quick treatment is critical.
There are two types of stroke: ischemic and hemorrhagic. A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is sometimes called a 'mini-stroke.'
cdc_fast_facts: In the United States in 2022, 1 in 6 deaths (17.5%) from cardiovascular disease was due to stroke.
The death rate for stroke decreased from 39.5 per 100,000 in 2022 to 39.0 per 100,000 in 2023.
Every 40 seconds, someone in the United States has a stroke. Every 3 minutes and 14 seconds, someone dies of stroke in this country.
Every year, more than 795,000 people in the United States have a stroke. About 610,000 of these are first or new strokes.
About 185,000 strokes — nearly 1 in 4 — are in people who have had a previous stroke.
About 87% of all strokes are ischemic strokes, in which blood flow to the brain is blocked.
Stroke-related costs in the United States came to nearly $56.2 billion between 2019 and 2020, including health care services, medicines, and missed days of work.
Stroke is a leading cause of serious long-term disability, and it reduces mobility in more than half of stroke survivors age 65 and older.
In 2014, 38% of people hospitalized for stroke were less than 65 years old.

cdc_types_detail.ischemic_stroke: Most strokes are ischemic strokes. An ischemic stroke occurs when blood clots or other particles block the blood vessels to the brain. Fatty deposits called plaque can also cause blockages by building up in the blood vessels.
cdc_types_detail.hemorrhagic_stroke: A hemorrhagic stroke happens when an artery in the brain leaks blood or ruptures (breaks open). The leaked blood puts too much pressure on brain cells, which damages them. High blood pressure and aneurysms — balloon-like bulges in an artery that can stretch and burst — are examples of conditions that can cause a hemorrhagic stroke.
cdc_types_detail.transient_ischemic_attack: TIAs are sometimes known as 'warning strokes.' A TIA is a warning sign of a future stroke and a medical emergency, just like a major stroke — blood flow to the brain is blocked for only a short time, usually no more than 5 minutes. There is no way to know at the beginning whether symptoms are from a TIA or a major stroke, and like ischemic strokes, blood clots often cause TIAs. More than a third of people who have a TIA and don't get treatment have a major stroke within 1 year; as many as 10% to 15% of people will have a major stroke within 3 months of a TIA. Recognizing and treating TIAs can lower the risk of a major stroke.

cdc_race_ethnicity_statistics: Stroke is a leading cause of death for Americans, and the risk of having a stroke varies with race and ethnicity.
Risk of having a first stroke is nearly twice as high for non-Hispanic Black adults as for White adults.
Non-Hispanic Black adults and Pacific Islander adults have the highest rates of death from stroke.
stroke.cdc_populations_note: High blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, obesity, and diabetes are leading causes of stroke. One in three US adults has at least one of these conditions or risk factors.
stroke.cdc_what_cdc_is_doing: CDC and its partners lead national initiatives and programs to reduce rates of death and disability from stroke and help people live longer, healthier lives. CDC's Division for Heart Disease and Stroke Prevention (DHDSP) provides resources to all 50 states, including: the WISEWOMAN program, which screens women aged 35 to 64 with low incomes and little or no insurance for chronic disease risk factors and refers them to lifestyle programs to prevent heart disease and stroke; and the Paul Coverdell National Acute Stroke Program, which funds states to measure, track, and improve the quality of care for stroke patients in order to reduce death and disability from stroke.

women_and_stroke.overview: Stroke is a leading cause of death for women. In the United States, 1 in 5 women between the ages of 55 and 75 will have a stroke. Many women do not know their risk of having a stroke, but 4 in 5 strokes are preventable.
risk_factors: High blood pressure (hypertension) is a main risk factor for stroke. More than 2 in 5 women in the United States have blood pressure greater than or equal to 130/80 mm Hg or are taking medicine to control their blood pressure; only about 1 in 4 of them have their blood pressure controlled to less than 130/80 mm Hg.
Stroke risk increases with age. Because women generally live longer than men, more women have strokes over their lifetimes.

Women also have unique risk factors for stroke, including: having high blood pressure during pregnancy; using certain types of birth control medicines, especially if they also smoke (about 1 in 9 women smoke); and having higher rates of depression.

at_risk_populations.african_american_women: Stroke is a leading cause of death among African American women, who are more likely to die from a stroke than non-Hispanic White women or Hispanic women in the United States. African American people have the highest rate of death due to stroke among all racial and ethnic groups. Almost 3 in 5 African American women are diagnosed with high blood pressure (greater than or equal to 130/80 mm Hg), a much higher proportion than White women (almost 2 in 5). African American women are diagnosed with higher rates of obesity (nearly 3 in 5) and diabetes (more than 1 in 8), conditions that increase the risk for stroke, than White women. US adults consume more than the recommended amount of salt or sodium, which raises blood pressure and increases the risk for stroke. Sickle cell disease, a common genetic disorder in African Americans, can lead to a stroke — about 1 in 365 African American babies are born with sickle cell disease. Smoking greatly increases stroke risk; about 1 in 8 African American women smoke.
at_risk_populations.hispanic_women: Stroke is the fourth leading cause of death for Hispanic women in the United States. High blood pressure is one of the main risk factors for a stroke — more than 1 in 3 Hispanic women have blood pressure above 130/90 mm Hg. People with diabetes are at higher risk for stroke; more than 1 in 9 Hispanic women have diabetes, and many don't know they have it. Among Hispanic adults, diabetes is most common in people of Mexican and Puerto Rican ancestry. Obesity increases the risk for stroke; about half of Hispanic women have obesity.

abcs_of_heart_and_brain_health: Aspirin: may help reduce risk for stroke by preventing blood clots — check with a doctor before taking aspirin to make sure it is right for you.
Blood pressure: control blood pressure with healthy lifestyle changes and take blood pressure medicines as directed.
Cholesterol: manage cholesterol with healthy lifestyle changes and take medicine as directed.
Smoking: don't start smoking; if you do smoke, learn how to quit.
lifestyle_changes: Eat healthy: choose healthy foods most of the time, with less salt/sodium to lower blood pressure, and foods rich in fiber and whole grains to manage cholesterol.
Get regular physical activity to reach and maintain a healthy weight and keep the heart and blood vessels healthier.

men_and_stroke.overview: Stroke is a leading cause of death among men and a leading cause of long-term disability. Men under age 44 are hospitalized for certain types of stroke at a higher rate than women in the same age group. About 4 in 5 strokes are preventable.
risk_factors: High blood pressure, also called hypertension, is a major risk factor for stroke. Half of men (50.6%) have high blood pressure greater than or equal to 130/80 mm Hg or are taking medicine for their blood pressure. Four out of 5 men with high blood pressure do not have their blood pressure controlled.
Smoking damages blood vessels, which can cause a stroke. About 1 in 7 men smoke, and men are also more likely to be smokers than women are.
Overweight and obesity increase stroke risk. About 3 in 4 men in the United States have overweight or obesity.
Diabetes increases stroke risk because it can harm blood vessels in the brain. About 1 in 7 men have diabetes.

Too much alcohol can raise blood pressure levels and increase the risk for stroke, and also increases triglycerides (a form of fat in the blood that can harden arteries). Men are more likely than women to drink too much alcohol.
Not enough physical activity can lead to other health conditions that increase the risk for stroke.

at_risk_populations.african_american_men: More than 1 in 2 African American men have a blood pressure greater than or equal to 130/80 mm Hg or are taking medicine to control their blood pressure. About 1 in 9 African American men have been diagnosed with diabetes, and many more have the disease but do not know it. Sickle cell disease, a common genetic disorder in African Americans, can lead to a stroke — about 1 in 365 African American babies are born with sickle cell disease. About 1 in 5 African American men smoke, and about 7 in 10 African American men have overweight or obesity. US adults, including African Americans, consume more than the recommended amounts of salt or sodium, which raises blood pressure and increases the risk for stroke.
at_risk_populations.hispanic_men: About half of Hispanic men have a blood pressure greater than or equal to 130/80 mm Hg or are taking medicine to lower blood pressure — a major risk factor for stroke. About 1 in 7 Hispanic men have been diagnosed with diabetes, and many more have the disease but do not know it; diabetes is also more common in people of Mexican and Puerto Rican ancestry than in people of Cuban or Central/South American ancestry. About 1 in 7 Hispanic men smoke, and more than 4 in 5 Hispanic men have overweight or obesity.

plague.name: Plague
plague.source: World Health Organization — Plague fact sheet
key_facts: Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, found naturally in small mammals and their fleas.
There are two main clinical forms: bubonic (most common) and pneumonic (most severe).
The case-fatality ratio for untreated bubonic plague is 30–60%, and untreated pneumonic plague is almost always fatal.
Effective antibiotic treatment exists — early diagnosis and treatment save lives.
The most endemic countries currently are the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Madagascar, and Peru.
plague.overview: Plague is a severe bacterial infection transmitted between animals and humans mainly through infected flea bites, though it can also spread through contact with infected tissue or by inhaling respiratory droplets from a person with pneumonic plague. It's historically known as the cause of the medieval 'Black Death,' but is easily treated with antibiotics today when caught early.

form_specific_symptoms.bubonic: A painful, swollen lymph node (called a bubo) typically near the site of the flea bite.
form_specific_symptoms.pneumonic: Severe respiratory illness that can progress rapidly, within as little as 24 hours, and can spread person-to-person through respiratory droplets.

plague.escalation_note: Any suspected case of plague is a medical emergency requiring immediate antibiotic treatment. Untreated pneumonic plague can be fatal within 18–24 hours, but survival rates are high if treatment starts within 24 hours of symptom onset.
prevention: Avoid contact with wild rodents and their fleas
Avoid handling animal carcasses
Use insect repellent and flea control measures in known risk areas
Use standard precautions (masks, hygiene) around anyone with suspected pneumonic plague
High-exposure workers such as lab or healthcare staff may be given preventive antibiotics
plague.treatment: Prompt antibiotic treatment combined with supportive care is effective if started early. Patients with pneumonic plague need to be isolated to prevent airborne spread to others.
