cdc_key_points: Plague is a potentially life-threatening disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
Plague is spread to people through bites from infected rodent fleas or, less often, direct contact with an infected animal.
Plague occurs naturally in parts of the western United States. Sudden illness or death among wild rodents, such as squirrels or prairie dogs, could indicate plague activity.
Plague can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment must be given quickly.

Plague is infamous for killing millions of people in Europe during the Middle Ages. Nowadays, it is a rare but persistent cause of illness in rural areas in the western United States and certain regions of Africa and Asia.

cdc_forms_detail.bubonic_plague: Patients develop fever, headache, chills, and weakness and one or more swollen, painful lymph nodes (called buboes). This form usually results from the bite of an infected flea, with an incubation period of 2 to 8 days. The bacteria multiply in a lymph node near where the bacteria entered the human body. If the patient is not treated with the appropriate antibiotics, the bacteria can spread to other parts of the body.
cdc_forms_detail.septicemic_plague: Patients develop fever, chills, extreme weakness, abdominal pain, shock, and possibly bleeding into the skin and other organs. Skin and other tissues may turn black and die, especially on fingers, toes, and the nose. Septicemic plague can occur as the first symptom of plague or may develop from untreated bubonic plague. This form results from bites of infected fleas or from handling an infected animal. The incubation period of septicemic plague is poorly defined but likely occurs within days of exposure.
cdc_forms_detail.pneumonic_plague: Patients develop fever, headache, weakness, and a rapidly developing pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, and sometimes bloody or watery mucous. Pneumonic plague develops when bacteria spread to the lungs of a patient with untreated bubonic or septicemic plague, or when a person inhales infectious droplets coughed out by another person or animal with pneumonic plague. Pneumonic plague is the most serious form of the disease and is the only form of plague that can be spread from person to person. The incubation period of pneumonic plague following inhalation can be as short as 1 day.

plague.cdc_when_to_talk_to_doctor: Plague is a serious illness. If you are experiencing symptoms like those listed here, seek immediate medical attention. Prompt treatment with the correct medications is critical to prevent complications or death.

cdc_how_it_spreads.flea_bites: Plague bacteria are most often transmitted by the bite of an infected flea. During plague epizootics, many rodents die, causing hungry fleas to seek other sources of blood. People and animals that visit places where rodents have recently died from plague are at risk of being infected from flea bites. Dogs and cats may also bring plague-infected fleas into the home. Flea bite exposure may result in primary bubonic or septicemic plague.
cdc_how_it_spreads.contact_with_contaminated_fluid_or_tissu: Humans can become infected when handling tissue or body fluids of a plague-infected animal — for example, a hunter skinning a rabbit or other infected animal without using proper precautions (e.g., gloves) could become infected with plague bacteria. This form of exposure most commonly results in bubonic plague or septicemic plague.
cdc_how_it_spreads.infectious_droplets: Humans and animals with plague pneumonia can sometimes cough droplets containing plague bacteria into the air. These bacteria-containing droplets can cause pneumonic plague in another person if inhaled. Typically, this requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague. Transmission of these droplets is the only way that plague can spread between people. Person-to-person spread has not been documented in the United States since 1924, but there continue to be rare cases of pneumonic plague among people exposed to sick cats. Cats are particularly susceptible to plague and can be infected by eating infected rodents. Cats with plague pose a risk of transmitting infectious plague droplets to their owners or to veterinarians.

plague.cdc_ecology: The bacteria that cause plague, Y. pestis, maintain their existence in a cycle involving rodents and their fleas. Plague occurs in rural and semi-rural areas of the western United States, primarily in semi-arid upland forests and grasslands where many types of rodent species can be involved — such as rock squirrels, wood rats, ground squirrels, prairie dogs, chipmunks, mice, voles, and rabbits. Wild carnivores can become infected by eating other infected animals. Scientists think that plague bacteria circulate at low rates within populations of certain rodents without causing excessive rodent die-off; these infected animals and their fleas serve as long-term reservoirs for the bacteria, called the enzootic cycle. Occasionally, other species become infected, causing an outbreak among animals, called an epizootic; humans are usually more at risk during, or shortly after, a plague epizootic. In parts of the developing world, plague can sometimes occur in urban areas with dense rat infestations. The last urban outbreak of rat-associated plague in the United States occurred in Los Angeles in 1924-1925.

cdc_diagnosis.diagnosis_overview: Plague is a plausible diagnosis for people who are sick and live in, or have recently traveled to, the western United States or any other plague-endemic area. The most common sign of bubonic plague is the rapid development of a swollen and painful lymph node called a bubo. A known flea bite or the presence of a bubo may help a doctor to consider plague as a cause of the illness. In many cases, particularly in septicemic and pneumonic plague, there are no obvious signs that indicate plague.
cdc_diagnosis.laboratory_testing: Diagnosis is made by taking samples from the patient, especially blood or part of a swollen lymph gland, and submitting them for laboratory testing. If plague is strongly suspected as the cause of illness, antibiotic treatment should begin as soon as samples are collected, without waiting for the final results.

plague.cdc_treatment_note: Plague is a very serious illness but treatable with commonly available antibiotics. The earlier a patient seeks medical care and receives appropriate treatment for plague, the better their chances of a full recovery.
cdc_prevention_tips: Reduce rodent habitat around your home, workplace, and recreational areas. Remove brush, rock piles, junk, cluttered firewood, and possible rodent food supplies, such as pet and wild animal food. Make your home and outbuildings rodent-proof.

Wear gloves if you are handling or skinning potentially infected animals to prevent contact between your skin and the plague bacteria. Contact your local health department if you have questions about disposal of dead animals.

Use repellent if you think you could be exposed to fleas during activities such as camping, hiking, or working outdoors. Products containing DEET can be applied to the skin as well as clothing, and products containing permethrin can be applied to clothing (always follow instructions on the label).

Keep fleas off of your pets by applying flea control products. Animals that roam freely are more likely to come in contact with plague-infected animals or fleas and could bring them into homes. If your pet becomes sick, seek care from a veterinarian as soon as possible.
Do not allow dogs or cats that roam free in endemic areas to sleep on your bed.
plague.cdc_vaccine_note: A plague vaccine is no longer available in the United States. New plague vaccines are in development but are not expected to be commercially available in the immediate future.

cdc_bioterrorism.overview: Plague is a potentially life-threatening disease caused by Yersinia pestis. It is possible that Y. pestis could be released intentionally in a biological attack to sicken people. Public health authorities, including CDC, have prepared for the possible but unlikely event that Y. pestis could be used as a biological weapon. Although the threat of a bioterrorist attack using Y. pestis is unlikely, there are examples throughout history of Y. pestis being used as a bioweapon. If such an emergency were to occur in the United States, CDC and other federal agencies would work closely with state and local partners to coordinate a response.
cdc_bioterrorism.how_cdc_would_respond: Several cases of pneumonic plague in one area would be a public health emergency, prompting CDC to respond immediately. Additionally, any case of plague outside areas where plague naturally occurs and in people without history of travel would cause alarm. In a plague emergency, CDC and other federal agencies would work closely with state and local partners to coordinate a response, including: coordinating activities through the Emergency Operations Center; communicating information about plague to the public; providing guidance to healthcare providers, hospitals, health departments, and others on how to respond; and working with the Laboratory Response Network (LRN) to test samples from sick people.

hiv_aids.name: HIV and AIDS
hiv_aids.source: World Health Organization — HIV and AIDS fact sheet
key_facts: HIV has claimed an estimated 44.2 million lives to date, with transmission ongoing in every country.
An estimated 41.0 million people were living with HIV at the end of 2025.
There is no cure for HIV, but with effective prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, it has become a manageable chronic condition.
People on effective antiretroviral treatment (ART) with an undetectable viral load do not transmit HIV to sexual partners.
hiv_aids.overview: HIV is a virus that attacks and weakens the immune system, making the body more vulnerable to infections and certain cancers. AIDS refers to the most advanced stage of untreated infection. HIV is spread through specific body fluids — blood, breast milk, semen, and vaginal fluids — and is not spread through everyday contact like hugging, kissing, or sharing food.
symptoms: Many people have no symptoms at all in the first weeks after infection.
Some experience a short flu-like illness: fever, headache, rash, sore throat.
As untreated infection progresses, symptoms can include swollen lymph nodes, weight loss, ongoing fever, diarrhoea, and cough.
Without treatment, HIV can eventually lead to severe illnesses such as tuberculosis, certain infections, and specific cancers.
hiv_aids.transmission: Through blood, breast milk, semen, and vaginal fluids of a person living with HIV, including from a mother to her baby during pregnancy or delivery. It is not spread by casual day-to-day contact.
prevention: Use condoms consistently during sex
Get tested regularly for HIV and other sexually transmitted infections
Consider pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) if at higher risk — available as a daily pill, vaginal ring, or long-acting injectable
Seek post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) promptly after a possible high-risk exposure
Use only sterile needles and injecting equipment
Pregnant women living with HIV should start ART as early as possible to protect their own health and prevent transmission to their baby
hiv_aids.escalation_note: Anyone with a recent high-risk exposure should seek medical advice promptly, ideally within hours to days, to discuss PEP. Anyone with symptoms suggestive of advanced, untreated HIV — persistent fever, major unexplained weight loss, or recurring infections — should see a healthcare provider for testing and care.
hiv_aids.treatment: There is no cure, but antiretroviral therapy (ART) stops the virus from replicating, allows the immune system to recover, and lets people living with HIV lead long, healthy lives. Treatment is lifelong and works best when started as early as possible after diagnosis.

clinical_reference_statpearls.source_note: NCBI Bookshelf — StatPearls, 'HIV and AIDS' (NBK534860), last updated January 14, 2026
clinical_reference_statpearls.overview: Clinical prevention of HIV and AIDS is the cornerstone of controlling the global HIV pandemic, which has claimed over 44.1 million lives worldwide since it was recognized. Although a cure remains out of reach, HIV is a chronic illness due to the effectiveness of antiretroviral therapy (ART). Combined with significant advancements in prevention, the goal of halting the global HIV pandemic is now considered feasible. HIV was first identified in 1983. Adequate resources and advances in prevention, treatment, and implementation science make the United Nations General Assembly's 95-95-95 goals attainable: in 2024, an estimated 87% of all people living with HIV knew their status, 89% of those who knew their status were receiving ART, and 94% of people on treatment had a suppressed viral load. Prior to a major disruption in funding, these statistics were getting close to the 2025 goals of 95% diagnosed, 95% of diagnosed on ART, and 95% of those on ART achieving viral suppression. Globally, HIV and mortality rates show a steady decrease, though some countries report an uptrend in infections, mostly where political or other turmoil is occurring or where HIV is highly stigmatized. With improvements in treatment, the number of patients with HIV is also increasing, with approximately 40.8 million people living with HIV and 1.3 million newly infected in 2024 — two-thirds of whom live in Africa.
clinical_reference_statpearls.clinical_costs_and_barriers: HIV imposes high costs on both patients and the healthcare system. Infection with HIV increases the risk of chronic disease, particularly cardiac and neurological. Although ART delays disease progression, treatment does not cure HIV, causes adverse effects, and requires consistent, prolonged connection to the healthcare system. Several barriers to universal treatment exist, including public and self-stigma, inadequate access to care, inappropriate care, and costs. Using local clinical guidelines for managing HIV improves patient outcomes and prevents HIV transmission. Increasing the involvement of community-led organizations in HIV testing and treatment, and integrating medical services for related health issues, extends service reach, improves linkage to care, and improves overall health.
clinical_reference_statpearls.etiology: HIV is part of the Retroviridae family in the Lentivirus genus. The virus mainly targets CD4+ T-lymphocyte helper cells, leading to extreme immune suppression with a continuous loss of cells. Untreated HIV eventually progresses to AIDS, at which stage the immune system cannot prevent infections, resulting in death due to opportunistic infections. There are two main types of HIV: HIV-1 and HIV-2. Although their genomes are structurally similar, they diverge significantly at the amino acid level — the two viruses result from two different zoonotic transmissions of simian immunodeficiency viruses, and are only 60% identical at the amino acid level and 48% identical at the nucleotide level, giving them substantial differences in severity, transmissibility, and prognosis. HIV-1 and HIV-2 particles comprise a lipid membrane surrounding a protein capsid, which holds a nucleoprotein core of 2 identical copies of RNA plus nucleocapsid, integrase, and reverse transcriptase proteins, organized into a lattice giving the capsid a characteristic conical shape. HIV is transmitted through body fluids such as blood, amniotic fluid, breast milk, semen, pre-ejaculate, rectal fluids, and vaginal fluids — via sexual contact, during pregnancy and delivery, and through fomites such as reusable medical equipment or syringes.

epidemiology_detailed.global_burden: According to the WHO HIV factsheet, there were 40.8 million patients with HIV at the end of 2024, with more than 60% living in Sub-Saharan Africa. In 2024, 1.3 million new cases of HIV were reported worldwide, with 630,000 deaths related to HIV in the same year. HIV-2 accounts for only 1 to 2 million prevalent infections, while HIV-1 accounts for the balance; HIV-2 exceeds 1% of infections only in Guinea-Bissau, Senegal, Gambia, Sierra Leone, and the Ivory Coast.
epidemiology_detailed.trends: Although some countries report an increase in new infections, the overall global trend in HIV incidence has decreased — there was a 40% decline in new HIV infections in 2024 compared to 2010. Significant gains were made in preventing and treating HIV in eastern and southern Africa, where the virus is most prevalent: from 2010 to 2023, there were 59% fewer new infections and 57% fewer AIDS-related deaths in the region. Progress is slower in other areas, mainly where marked inequities and low prioritization of the HIV response exist. Between 2010 and 2022 in Asia and the Pacific region, where the largest epidemic after eastern and southern Africa exists, new HIV infections increased by 32% among men who have sex with men and by 85% among non-client sex partners of key populations, while a comparable regional epidemic increased by 94% between 2019 and 2024. Challenging legal environments, human rights violations, and military conflicts have hindered the HIV response in some regions.
epidemiology_detailed.sex_and_key_populations: HIV diagnosis, treatment, and viral suppression rates vary across and within countries and regions. Globally, women and girls accounted for 45% of new HIV cases in 2024. However, diagnosis, treatment access, and viral suppression rates are lower among men than women: 84% vs 92%, 87% vs 91%, and 94% vs 95%, respectively. UNAIDS and WHO identify 5 key populations who are disproportionately affected by HIV and warrant specific care and support to reduce global transmissions: gay men and other men who have sex with men, sex workers, people in prisons and other closed settings, people who inject drugs, and transgender people.
epidemiology_detailed.transmission_patterns: The vast majority of new HIV cases worldwide occur from sexual contact. Most of these infections are transmitted through heterosexual contact due to the high number of infections in Africa, where this mode of transmission is dominant. Most new HIV diagnoses in most other regions of the world occur in men who have sex with men — in the United States in 2022, 67% of all new infections were in men who have sex with men.
epidemiology_detailed.us_statistics: US statistics show that in 2021, 87% of persons living with HIV were diagnosed, 82% of them were linked to care within a month of HIV diagnosis, and 66% of those diagnosed were virally suppressed. The median CD4 count at the time of treatment initiation was 364 cells/µL.
epidemiology_detailed.drug_use_as_risk_factor: Drug use is another significant risk factor for HIV. According to a meta-analysis from 2023, approximately 2.25 million people who inject drugs are living with HIV worldwide. According to the CDC, in 2022, 7% of new HIV cases in the United States could be attributed to injection drug use, either alone or in men who have sex with men who report injection drug use. A systematic review evaluating the effectiveness of needle and syringe exchange programs reported that adequate programs are effective in reducing the sharing and reuse of needles and syringes and HIV transmission among people who inject drugs.

clinical_reference_statpearls.pathophysiology_detailed: The Retroviridae family is unique among viruses, with the RNA viral genome reverse-transcribed into DNA before being integrated into the host DNA, resulting in lifelong infection. As the primary host cellular receptor for HIV-1 and HIV-2 is the CD4+ antigen, T cells and macrophages that express CD4+ are the primary viral targets. Envelope glycoprotein on the surface of the viral particle facilitates viral entry into the host cell; chemokine coreceptors CCR5 and CXCR4 on the host cell surface trigger a conformational change in the envelope protein, resulting in fusion of the viral and host cellular membranes and release of the viral capsid into the host cell. The HIV-1 capsid remains intact or nearly intact until reaching the nuclear pore complexes; reverse transcription is now believed to occur during or shortly after the capsid is imported into the nucleus, though its precise location and mechanism are not fully elucidated. The viral reverse transcriptase enzyme initiates reverse transcription using host transfer RNA as primers; the viral integrase protein then somewhat randomly integrates the resulting double-stranded DNA into the host DNA. Within 2 days of initial mucosal exposure, HIV can be detected in regional lymph node tissue, and from there the virus only requires 3 days to be detected in the plasma. Genomic diversification is an important aspect of HIV pathogenesis, leading to changes in disease severity and response to ART — a primary driving factor is the high error rate of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (100 to 1000 times higher than cellular DNA polymerases for group M subtype B), with recombination errors, host restriction factors, and depletion of host deoxynucleoside triphosphates also contributing to viral mutagenesis and ART failure. In the initial phase of infection, viral replication is rampant, with an exponential increase in plasma HIV RNA due to the large population of susceptible CD4+ T cells without any host immune response; a significant decline from the peak viremia level then occurs due to the HIV-specific immune response from cytotoxic CD8+ T cells. Follicular regulatory T cells are believed to be involved in poor humoral immunity and HIV persistence in patients treated with ART, and follicular CD8+ cytotoxic T cells are relatively less abundant compared to their extrafollicular counterparts in patients with HIV, likewise believed to contribute to disrupted immunogenesis.
clinical_reference_statpearls.histopathology: Lymphadenopathy exhibiting distinctive morphological changes is evident in patients with HIV. In untreated cases, pronounced follicular hyperplasia emerges initially, marked by enlarged, irregularly shaped follicles with absent or dramatically decreased mantle cell zones, centroblasts as the dominant cell type, a starry-sky appearance of the germinal centers, follicle lysis or fragmentation, and sinusoidal monocytoid B-cell hyperplasia. Mixed follicular hyperplasia is the intermediate stage between florid hyperplasia and follicular involution. In follicular involution, small, atrophic, and hypocellular follicles are observed, with hyalinized follicular dendritic cell meshworks, few germinal center B cells, hyalinized blood vessels penetrating the follicles, an expanded interfollicular area with a washed-out appearance, and abundant histiocytes and polytypic plasma cells. Eventually, the lymph nodes enter the lymphocyte-depletion stage, characterized by loss of germinal centers and a near absence of lymphocytes, with the interfollicular area primarily consisting of histiocytes, plasma cells, and a few immunoblasts, and focal hyaline deposits with subcapsular and sinusoidal fibrosis may be present. Lymph nodes, along with the central nervous system and reproductive tracts, may serve as 'sanctuary sites' where antiretrovirals do not penetrate well and where the virus may continue replicating at low levels, making it difficult to eliminate the virus.
clinical_reference_statpearls.history_and_physical: A medical history and physical examination include a review of systems for patients with confirmed or suspected HIV, with attention to signs and symptoms that rule out other conditions in the differential diagnosis and that signal opportunistic infections or HIV-associated sequelae. In addition to characterizing symptoms, the history identifies risk factors for HIV transmission in a nonjudgmental manner, including sexual contact and behavior, drug use, and blood transfusions. The sexual history should elucidate the number of partners, sexual practices, frequency and type of barrier protection, previous history of sexually transmitted infections, and the HIV status of current and past partners. The drug use history should include the type and frequency of substances used, means of administration, and source and sharing of equipment. A mental health assessment is essential for identifying conditions such as depression, other mental illnesses, or substance use that may result in barriers to care or contribute to chronic disease. Obtaining an immunization history is crucial to determine which vaccines could offer future protection — for instance, against Streptococcus pneumoniae (associated with adverse outcomes in HIV-positive individuals) and hepatitis B (linked to a heightened risk of hepatocellular carcinoma progression in patients with HIV). Social history provides insight into the patient's perceptions of and ability to adhere to treatment and potential barriers to connection to healthcare services, including living situation, income, insurance, social support, experiences of stigma, coping strategies, and exposure to sexual or other violence.
clinical_reference_statpearls.staging_systems: The United States National Institutes of Health (NIH) describes 3 broad stages of HIV that develop over time: acute HIV, chronic HIV, and AIDS. The CDC maintains a staging system based on CD4+ count and AIDS-defining illnesses intended for surveillance. The WHO has a staging system based on clinical presentation for clinical or surveillance purposes in areas with limited or no availability of CD4+ testing.

acute_hiv.overview: Approximately 90% of patients with acute HIV experience at least 1 symptom within the first 4 weeks after primary HIV infection. These symptoms are typically mild, nonspecific, and self-limited. Some patients present with more severe symptoms, known as acute retroviral syndrome or seroconversion illness. A patient presenting with fever and a maculopapular rash a few weeks after potential exposure to HIV should be tested for the virus and promptly initiated on ART if positive.
acute_hiv.timing_and_prognosis: Symptom onset occurs acutely, approximately 2 to 4 weeks (range 4 days to 8 weeks) after viral infection, just before the peak of viremia. Symptom resolution typically lasts 18 days, coinciding with the establishment of a viral replication set point approximately 30 days after the initial viremia. Without treatment, higher viral load and increased severity and duration of conversion illness are early predictors of a poor prognosis. Mucocutaneous ulceration is a characteristic feature of acute HIV, characterized by shallow, sharply demarcated ulcers with a white base surrounded by a thin area of erythema — depending on the mode of transmission, ulcers may be located on the oral, anal, penile, or esophageal mucosa. Acute aseptic meningoencephalitis is reported as a clinical presentation of acute HIV-1.

clinical_reference_statpearls.chronic_hiv: After HIV acquisition and subsequent setting of the viral set point, patients enter the chronic phase of the infection. Most patients with chronic HIV remain asymptomatic before developing AIDS; however, nonspecific fatigue may present, and persistent generalized lymphadenopathy is usual, characterized by at least 2 noncontiguous sites (other than inguinal nodes) exhibiting enlarged lymph nodes for more than 3 to 6 months, not explained by other lymphoproliferative or infectious causes. Patients with chronic HIV without AIDS can develop oropharyngeal candidiasis, recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, oral hairy leukoplakia, disseminated cutaneous herpes simplex virus, and cervical dysplasia or cervical carcinoma in situ. Cutaneous manifestations such as seborrheic dermatitis, bacillary angiomatosis, varicella-zoster virus reactivations, and molluscum contagiosum infections are common and tend to be severe in patients with HIV.

aids_defining_conditions.overview: Eventually, HIV progresses to advanced disease, particularly if left untreated or inadequately treated. AIDS is diagnosed when specific AIDS-defining conditions are noted, regardless of the CD4+ count. These AIDS-defining conditions, outlined by the CDC, tend to occur most frequently with low CD4+ counts (<200 cells/mm³), which correlates with untreated advanced HIV as the total lymphocyte count depletes over time.
conditions: Candidiasis of the digestive tract (other than thrush)
Extrapulmonary or disseminated coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, or cryptococcosis, including cryptococcal meningitis
HIV encephalitis and HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder

evaluation_and_testing.overview: Testing is essential to confirm a diagnosis of HIV. Antibody, antigen-antibody, and nucleic acid amplification tests are available for screening or confirming HIV. No currently available testing technology can detect HIV during the initial phase of infection because viral levels in the blood are too low — this period, known as the eclipse period, lasts approximately 10 days. During the window phase, lasting up to 20-25 days after infection, and subsequently, the virus may be detected by nucleic acid amplification tests (detecting HIV RNA as early as 6 to 8 days after infection), antigen tests (detecting viral proteins such as p24 antigen as early as 13 to 20 days after infection), or antigen-antibody tests (detecting viral proteins with other antigen tests, plus anti-HIV IgM and IgG antibodies around 20 and 30 days, respectively, after infection).
evaluation_and_testing.testing_algorithm: Detection during the window period is unreliable, but once seroconversion (antibody positivity) occurs, the window period ends. In clinical settings, combination antigen/antibody (Ag/Ab) tests are recommended to identify patients with HIV; ideally, the Ag/Ab test should be a fourth-generation test capable of detecting HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies and the HIV-1 p24 antigen. If the initial positive test cannot distinguish between HIV-1 and HIV-2, a supplemental antibody immunoassay is required. All initial positive test results are followed by a second HIV test, preferably a laboratory-based test, to confirm a diagnosis of HIV; the false positive rate of third- and fourth-generation tests is very low. If the combination assay result is negative, no further testing is indicated unless HIV exposure is too recent for p24 antigen levels to reach detectable levels. If the initial Ag/Ab test result is negative and early HIV is suspected, an HIV-1 nucleic acid amplification test should be performed. Specimens that are indeterminate on the initial Ag/Ab test, or nonreactive or indeterminate with the HIV-1- and HIV-2-specific antibody assay, are followed by an HIV-1 nucleic acid amplification test. An acute HIV case is diagnosed with a positive nucleic acid amplification test result or p24 antigen in the setting of a negative or indeterminate HIV antibody result; while subsequent confirmation of HIV antibody seroconversion is required, persons diagnosed with acute HIV should be treated with ART immediately due to high viremia.
baseline_labs_after_diagnosis: Quantitative plasma HIV-1 RNA viral load
Complete blood count, glucose, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, liver enzymes, bilirubin, urinalysis, serum lipids, and serology for hepatitis A, B, and C viruses

Genotypic drug-resistance assessment focusing on genes for reverse transcriptase and protease in treatment-naive people, with the addition of integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) resistance testing for patients previously treated with ARTs or CAB-LA PrEP

Other tests as indicated based on history and physical examination, such as testing for sexually transmitted infections (Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, syphilis serology), opportunistic infections, or cancer
evaluation_and_testing.monitoring_notes: Viral load is the most important indicator of initial and sustained response to ART and aids in ART selection; it should be monitored at entry into care, initiation of therapy, and periodically afterward. CD4+ counts are the best indicators of immune function, disease progression, and survival, and determine the need to initiate prophylaxis for opportunistic infections. Blood must be drawn for CD4+ testing before starting ART, but ART should not be delayed pending results; if CD4+ is unavailable, the WHO staging system should be used. Monitoring inflammatory markers or other CD subsets is not recommended due to cost and limited clinical utility. Routine testing for herpes simplex IgG, cytomegalovirus IgG, and toxoplasma IgG is not recommended, as these tests do not distinguish active disease from prior exposure. Testing for serum cryptococcal antigen should be considered in patients with a CD4+ count of 100 cells/mm³ or less.

treatment_management.goal_and_general_approach: The goal of HIV-1 therapy with antiretroviral medications is to achieve sustained virologic suppression (<50 copies/mL). According to current WHO and CDC guidelines, ART should begin after the diagnosis of HIV is confirmed (including upon confirmation of acute HIV) and an initial assessment, regardless of immune status or clinical stage, unless a severe opportunistic infection is present. Management of HIV must include identifying specific support required by the patient to maintain medication adherence; treatment selection is based on patient preferences and the ability to adhere to a medication regimen.

drug_classes.overview: Nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs), and protease inhibitors (PIs) are used in treatment-naive patients. NRTIs inhibit viral replication by mimicking nucleotides and blocking viral reverse transcriptase, terminating DNA elongation in both HIV-1 and HIV-2 infections. NNRTIs block DNA prolongation by binding the viral reverse transcriptase at a separate site but are only active against HIV-1. INSTIs inhibit the transcribed viral DNA from integrating into the host genome. Protease inhibitors block the last step in the viral maturation process, rendering assembled viral particles immature and noninfectious. Other drug classes, such as CCR5 antagonists, fusion inhibitors, attachment inhibitors, capsid inhibitors, and post-attachment inhibitors, are reserved for patients with multidrug-resistant HIV.
nrtis: Abacavir (contraindicated for patients who are HLA-B*5701 positive)
Tenofovir (tenofovir alafenamide or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate)

treatment_management.recommended_therapy_treatment_naive: Current guidelines recommend initiating INSTI-based therapy with a dual NRTI backbone before conducting further laboratory testing for most patients with HIV. Tenofovir plus lamivudine or emtricitabine are the preferred NRTIs, and bictegravir and dolutegravir are the preferred INSTIs due to their effectiveness, adverse-effect profiles, shorter time to virological suppression, and lower propensity to develop resistance. Classically, three-drug regimens were necessary to prevent virologic failure due to the selection of drug-resistant viruses. In select cases where the HIV RNA level is <500,000 copies/mL, there is no genotypic resistance, and no coinfection with hepatitis B virus, a 2-drug regimen with dolutegravir and lamivudine is now considered first-line. INSTI-based regimens achieve faster viral suppression than protease inhibitor- or NNRTI-containing regimens. The addition of other agents in the setting of advanced HIV on presentation does not improve clinical outcomes at the onset of treatment and is not recommended. Abacavir is no longer recommended as initial therapy due to its association with cardiovascular disease, the risk of hypersensitivity, and the need for HLA-B*5701 testing. Antiretroviral treatment should be started regardless of the CD4+ count to reduce a combination of serious AIDS- and non-AIDS-related events and death from any cause if started at diagnosis compared to a deferred initiation of treatment; additionally, early ART reduces ongoing transmission of HIV to sexual partners. For patients unable to take an INSTI-based regimen, an antiretroviral from another class is prescribed — for example, the protease inhibitor darunavir boosted with cobicistat, ritonavir, or an NNRTI, either efavirenz or rilpivirine.

comorbid_conditions_affecting_art_select.hepatitis_b_coinfection: Tenofovir-containing ART regimens are preferred, as tenofovir suppresses hepatitis B virus replication. ART regimens that use lamivudine or emtricitabine without tenofovir should be avoided, as they can result in the rapid emergence of resistant hepatitis B virus.
comorbid_conditions_affecting_art_select.renal_dysfunction: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate is associated with proximal tubular dysfunction and should be avoided in patients with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of less than 50 mL/min/1.73 m². Tenofovir alafenamide can be used unless the patient has reduced renal function (estimated glomerular filtration rate <30 mL/min/1.73 m²) and is not on dialysis, in which case no tenofovir formulation is indicated — the preferred regimen is dolutegravir plus lamivudine, adjusted for renal function. Atazanavir should also be avoided in patients with reduced kidney function.
comorbid_conditions_affecting_art_select.osteoporosis: Tenofovir alafenamide is associated with less bone loss and is preferred over tenofovir disoproxil fumarate-containing regimens.
comorbid_conditions_affecting_art_select.pregnancy: Bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine, and dolutegravir or darunavir-ritonavir with a dual NRTI backbone, are preferred regimens. Doravirine, long-acting injectable cabotegravir plus rilpivirine, and cobicistat-containing regimens should not be used as initial regimens during pregnancy, mostly due to concerns for inadequate drug levels.

treatment_management.recommended_therapy_treatment_experience: Treatment-experienced patients require a wider range of antiviral options compared to initial treatment due to an increased probability of multidrug-resistant strains of HIV. While drug-resistance testing for transmitted virus needs to be monitored to select empiric initial ART, it is more important for treatment-experienced patients who fail ART. Databases such as the Stanford database and WHO reports monitor antiretroviral drug resistance globally. The barrier to resistance is higher with combination antiretroviral therapy containing later-generation integrase inhibitors such as dolutegravir and bictegravir. Common resistance mutations identified at the initiation of antiretroviral therapy in treatment-experienced patients include M184V and K65R with tenofovir, K103N/S in NNRTIs, and thymidine-analogue mutations in NRTIs. These patients still require 2 to 3 active agents against HIV to reduce the risk of virological failure and drug resistance. Results from the NADIA, VISEND, and ARTIST trials changed WHO policy: these studies found that, despite viral resistance to NRTIs, patients failing NNRTI-based first-line regimens responded to dolutegravir-based regimens that recycled tenofovir and lamivudine or emtricitabine, implying that a drug-resistance assay was unnecessary before making this switch in resource-constrained settings. If a patient experiences failure of a dolutegravir-based regimen, the WHO recommends a boosted protease inhibitor-based regimen. US guidelines are similar for patients failing first-line therapy, with the following additions for second-line ART: an alternative to dolutegravir is bictegravir, the preferred protease inhibitor is ritonavir-boosted darunavir, and a third alternative is a 2-drug boosted PI plus an INSTI. A genotypic drug-resistance assay is indicated when the patient is still taking the ART or as soon as possible after ART discontinuation. For select treatment-experienced patients, separate from the issue of drug-resistance, an 8-weekly dosed regimen of injectable long-acting cabotegravir-rilpivirine is a potentially attractive full-ART option — criteria include sustained undetectable HIV RNA levels for more than 3 months, no known or suspected resistance to either cabotegravir or rilpivirine, and no active hepatitis B virus infection. The challenge with antiretroviral agent resistance is that it may not accurately predict clinical outcomes. In cases of complex drug resistance, more expensive phenotypic assays rather than genotypic assays may be considered for testing drug susceptibility against HIV. Patients who acquire HIV after receiving cabotegravir for preexposure prophylaxis require INSTI genotyping before beginning therapy with an INSTI-based regimen; while results are pending, a boosted protease inhibitor regimen containing darunavir and a tenofovir-based dual NRTI coformulation should be used.
treatment_management.hiv_2_therapy_considerations: Current recommendations for treating HIV-2 are primarily based on single-arm or observational studies, as most research and treatment efforts have focused on HIV-1. The initial regimen for managing HIV-2 should include 2 NRTIs plus a second-generation INSTI or a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and emtricitabine are the preferred NRTIs. Dolutegravir is recommended as the preferred INSTI. Darunavir and lopinavir are more active against HIV-2 compared to other protease inhibitors and are the preferred agents. Two-drug regimens to treat HIV-1 and any regimen containing NNRTIs are ineffective against HIV-2 and should not be used in these infections. Drug-resistance assays for HIV-2 are limited to research laboratories, complicating the management of these infections. Current data suggest that HIV-2 is susceptible to NRTIs; however, HIV-2 is more likely to develop resistance compared to HIV-1. Patients with HIV-2 mutations may exhibit complex patterns of protease inhibitor cross-resistance, making sequential regimens ineffective for patients with this infection. Clinical data regarding mutations and efficacy of the most commonly used INSTI, such as dolutegravir, are limited, especially in those previously exposed to other INSTIs.

opportunistic_infections.overview: The incidence of opportunistic infections in persons living with HIV has drastically reduced since the introduction of ART in the mid-1990s. The lower a patient's CD4+ T cell count, the greater the risk of diseases caused by opportunistic infections. In addition to ART, prophylaxis for opportunistic infections should be initiated according to the level of immunosuppression.
prophylaxis_thresholds: Pneumocystis jirovecii: Prophylaxis is indicated for patients with a CD4+ count of less than 200 cells/mm³ or a CD4+ count <14% (the CD4% criterion is for children under 12 years of age).
Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii: Patients with a CD4+ count of less than 100 cells/mm³ and a positive serum cryptococcal antigen result require prophylaxis.

Mycobacterium avium complex infection: If patients with HIV are rapidly initiated on ART, prophylaxis is not required. Patients with a CD4+ count of less than 50 cells/mm³ who are not receiving ART, or who remain viremic on ART, should receive prophylaxis.
Toxoplasma gondii: Patients with CD4+ counts less than 100 cells/mm³ who have positive test results for toxoplasma antibodies require chemoprophylaxis.
opportunistic_infections.immune_reconstitution_inflammatory_syndr: In patients with a severe opportunistic infection, rapid initiation of ART can result in immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). The opportunistic infection should be treated before initiating ART to decrease this risk. ART should generally be initiated within 2 weeks of treatment initiation for most acute opportunistic infections, except acute cryptococcal meningitis — patients with cryptococcal meningitis may commence HIV therapy 4 to 6 weeks after starting antifungal therapy. HIV treatment should be initiated within 2 weeks of tuberculosis treatment in patients who have active tuberculosis, especially if they have severe immunosuppression (CD4+ count <50 cells/mm³); however, if evidence of tuberculous meningitis is detected, ART should be initiated 4-8 weeks after starting anti-tuberculous treatment and given with high-dose corticosteroid treatment.
opportunistic_infections.recommended_prophylaxis_therapy: Prophylaxis and treatment of opportunistic infections in HIV-infected patients depend on the patient's level of immunosuppression and the identification of any causative pathogen; improving the underlying cause of the immunosuppression by treating HIV with ART is the best way to prevent opportunistic infections. Given the high risk of Pneumocystis jirovecii with CD4+ counts <200 cells/mm³ or a CD4+ count <14%, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) prophylaxis is recommended — in addition to preventing Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP), it also protects against cerebral toxoplasmosis, bacterial infections, and malaria in endemic settings. Alternatives for sulfa allergy where desensitization is not feasible include inhaled pentamidine, dapsone, or atovaquone; hypoglycemia must be monitored with the administration of pentamidine, whereas G6PD deficiency needs to be assessed before starting dapsone, and atovaquone can be considered but may not be as efficacious. Prophylaxis is often discontinued after the CD4+ count returns to >200 CD4+ cells/mm³ for 3 or more months in patients on antiretroviral therapy. In addition to reducing exposure to toxoplasmosis by avoiding raw or undercooked meats and a cat's litterbox, toxoplasmosis is prevented in patients with a CD4+ count <100 cells/mm³ by administering low-dose prophylactic therapy.

viral_suppression_and_resistance.monitoring: After treatment is initiated, the patient's HIV viral load should be evaluated in 4-8 weeks. Virologic suppression to undetectable levels (defined as an HIV RNA level of <200 copies/mL) may take up to 24 weeks of continuous therapy. When viral suppression is established, the viral load should be monitored every 3 to 4 months. An HIV RNA level that remains persistently below this lower limit of detection demonstrates sustained virologic suppression — the primary goal of HIV therapy. If the viral load is unsuppressed and adherence is confirmed, evaluation for resistance with genotype testing for the patient's regimen is recommended to identify a regimen that will control the virus.
viral_suppression_and_resistance.inadequate_suppression_and_resistance: When inadequate viral suppression occurs, the HIV viral load and selection pressure increase, inducing mutations favorable to resistance against antiretroviral drugs. The WHO defines virologic failure as when the viral load is above 1000 copies/mL on 2 separate and consecutive measurements over 3 months while on current antiretroviral treatment for 6 months or longer. The NIH defines virologic failure as the inability to achieve or maintain suppression of viral replication to an HIV RNA level <200 copies/mm³. This condition can result in clinical failure, described as a new event or recurrence of WHO stage 4 severe immunodeficiency after 6 months of current effective antiretroviral treatment; clinical failure suggests resistance to antiretroviral drugs in an adherent patient. Given that HIV has an RNA genome prone to mutations, selection pressure from active antiretroviral agents during reverse transcription can encourage drug-resistant mutants that lead to virological failure, clinical failure, and eventually immunological failure, defined as a CD4+ count of 250 cells/mm³ or less. Trials such as NADIA and REVAMP indicated that treatment regimens incorporating antiretroviral agents with prior resistance are feasible, though the theoretical basis of how HIV develops new mutations with inadequate viral suppression should be considered by the treating clinician in managing treatment-experienced patients.
viral_suppression_and_resistance.immunological_recovery: In patients who had a baseline CD4+ count of 250 cells/mm³ or less at diagnosis or immunological failure while on antiretroviral treatment but then subsequently recovered a CD4+ count at or above 500 cells/mm³, immunological recovery constitutes only a minority of all patients on effective antiretroviral treatment. The reasons are often multifactorial, including adherence, baseline CD4+ count at diagnosis, patient age and sex, the type of initial antiretroviral agents initiated at diagnosis and any delays, and the patient's baseline functional status. When immunological recovery occurs, it typically takes many months to years and depends on multiple factors, including the class of antiretroviral therapy, the patient's baseline functional status, and treatment adherence. Conversely, inadequate immunological responses are associated with an increased risk of serious non-AIDS-related morbidity and mortality in patients with HIV.

toxicity_and_adverse_effect_management.overview: When prescribing antiretrovirals, a wide variety of potential drug-drug interactions, toxicities, and other adverse effects must be considered; consultation with a pharmacologist is recommended.
nrti_adverse_effects: Abacavir is contraindicated for patients who are positive for the HLA-B*5701 allele due to the risk of hypersensitivity reactions; pretesting is required before prescribing any regimen containing abacavir, and some studies have also demonstrated increased cardiovascular risk with abacavir.
Tenofovir alafenamide is associated with higher lipid levels and weight gain, but it is associated with less renal toxicity compared to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate.

Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate is associated with renal toxicity, proximal tubulopathies such as Fanconi syndrome, and acute or chronic renal insufficiency, particularly when combined with booster agents.

fungal_diseases.name: Fungal Diseases
fungal_diseases.source: U.S. CDC — Fungal Diseases (About, Treatment, Health Equity, and FungiNet pages)
key_facts: Fungal diseases range from mild skin infections to deadly illnesses such as fungal meningitis.
People with weakened immune systems, including those with HIV/AIDS, are at greatest risk of severe illness and death from fungal diseases.

Fungal diseases disproportionately affect Black, American Indian or Alaska Native, and Hispanic persons, who have higher rates of fungal deaths compared with other groups — a disparity that was especially pronounced during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Antifungal medications (antifungals) tend to cause more side effects and often need to be taken for longer periods than antibiotics or antivirals.
New antifungal development is needed, since treatment options remain limited.
fungal_diseases.overview: Fungal diseases are caused by fungi that can be found in air, dust, and soil. Many fungal infections share symptoms with more common bacterial or viral infections, which can lead to misdiagnosis, since antibiotics and antivirals cannot treat fungal infections. Some disease-causing fungi are more common in certain parts of the world, so travel history matters for diagnosis.

hiv_aids_link.overview: People with HIV/AIDS are at increased risk for fungal diseases and have a higher risk for more severe forms of infection. Cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, and Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) are especially more likely to affect people with HIV. In the United States, Anti-Retroviral Therapy (ART) has substantially reduced the number of fungal diseases and deaths among people with HIV/AIDS since the 1990s — one study showed the incidence of cryptococcosis among people with HIV decreased by approximately 90% in the 1990s. However, ART does not eliminate the risk, so prevention efforts should continue. Fungal diseases remain common and deadly in parts of the world without widespread ART access, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Latin America.
risk_reduction: Maintain CD4 counts above 200 to help avoid serious illness from fungal infections.
Comply with antiretroviral therapy (ART), which helps slow the progress of HIV and helps prevent fungal infections.
Understand the range of severity — some fungal infections are mild skin rashes, but others, like fungal meningitis, can be deadly, so seek treatment as soon as possible.
Ask a healthcare provider specifically about fungal diseases if a prescribed antibiotic or antiviral is not working, since these cannot treat fungal infections.
Understand geographic risks — some disease-causing fungi are more common in certain parts of the world (see CDC's Traveler's Health site for travel-related illness information).
Avoid risky activities that increase dust and soil in the air, such as gardening, construction, and being outside in heavy winds, since disease-causing fungi live in air, dust, and soil.

Be aware of medication effects — some medications can increase risk for fungal infections such as thrush (an infection in the mouth and throat) which, while not life-threatening, can make eating painful.

prevention_strategies.preventative_medications: Healthcare providers sometimes prescribe TMP-SMX (also called Bactrim, Septra, or Cotrim) to prevent Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) in people with HIV/AIDS.
prevention_strategies.targeted_screening: Cryptococcal meningitis is a significant risk with a high death rate for people living with HIV/AIDS, particularly among those without ART. In areas where Cryptococcus and HIV are both common, targeted screening programs can detect the fungus in the body before it causes symptoms, allowing people who test positive to take antifungal medications preventively.

us_and_global_trends.united_states: ART has substantially reduced deaths caused by fungal diseases among people with HIV/AIDS in the U.S. since the 1980s, but ART does not eliminate the risk, so healthcare providers and people with HIV should still work to prevent infections.
us_and_global_trends.global: Fungal diseases are still a major risk and cause of death among people with HIV in some parts of the world. The two most common fungal disease risks are cryptococcosis and histoplasmosis. Worldwide, approximately 220,000 cases of cryptococcal meningitis and 181,000 deaths occur each year, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa. In Latin America, histoplasmosis is common, and approximately 30% of HIV/AIDS patients diagnosed with histoplasmosis die from this infection. Although access to HIV care and treatment is improving in developing countries, the need to increase and expand capacity continues.

treatment_with_antifungals.overview: Antifungals are medications that treat fungal diseases by killing or stopping the growth of fungal cells. Because fungal cells are similar to human cells, medications that harm fungal cells can also harm people, which is part of why antifungals tend to cause more and worse side effects among more people than other antimicrobials, and often need to be taken for longer periods — sometimes months or years — to fully treat an infection.
common_side_effects: Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea
severe_side_effects: Liver toxicity with certain azole antifungals
treatment_with_antifungals.appropriate_use: Antifungals should always be taken as directed by a healthcare provider or product label instructions. Inappropriate use can delay or prevent treatment of the infection, increase side effects, or contribute to the development of antimicrobial resistance. Always take the full prescribed amount and continue the medication for the whole instructed period even if feeling better. Talk to a healthcare provider if an antifungal causes serious side effects or symptoms do not improve.
treatment_with_antifungals.topical_antifungals_note: If buying a topical antifungal over the counter, choose a product that does NOT contain a corticosteroid or steroid. Corticosteroids and steroids are often combined in topical antifungals and can cause side effects and worsen fungal skin infections. This information is not widely known — talk to a healthcare provider if concerned about a prescribed topical antifungal.
treatment_with_antifungals.therapeutic_drug_monitoring: Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM) is a practice healthcare providers use to help find and adjust antifungal doses, since it can be challenging to find a dose that treats the infection while minimizing side effects. The provider monitors the level of drug in the patient's bloodstream, their treatment progress, and side effects at specific times. This matters because fungi can cause severe infections in any part of the body, including the brain and bloodstream, while medications strong enough to harm fungal cells can also harm human cells.
treatment_with_antifungals.future_directions: Scientists and researchers are working on new types of antifungals that could be more effective and treat infections more quickly than existing options, since treatment options remain limited.

health_equity.why_it_matters: Social differences like living conditions, income, occupation, and access to care can create health inequities. Fungal diseases can affect anyone, but people with weakened immune systems are at greatest risk of severe illness and death. Fungal diseases disproportionately affect Black, American Indian or Alaska Native, and Hispanic persons, who have higher rates of fungal deaths compared with other groups — a disparity that was especially pronounced during the COVID-19 pandemic. These disparities are likely driven in large part by inequities in the social determinants of health (SDOH) — the conditions of the places where people live, work, and play that affect health risks and outcomes. Some fungal diseases also affect some populations more than others based on biological conditions like sex, race, and ethnicity.
health_equity.what_prevents_health_equity: Differences in social determinants of health can lead to health inequities and increase fungal disease impact on some populations. For example, people who work outdoors in certain areas are more likely to inhale fungal spores from the environment. Health inequities affecting other health conditions can have a ripple effect: the risk for diabetes is higher among people living in areas with poor access to nutritious food and healthcare, and diabetes is itself a risk factor for several fungal diseases.

cdc_priorities.priority_1_expand_data_and_research: Data on the epidemiology of fungal diseases across demographic and geographic populations can help identify factors that drive inequities. Surveys, interviews, and focus groups with clinicians and affected populations can shed light on perspectives and barriers to health equity. Current projects examine the relationship between fungal diseases and social determinants (using the Social Vulnerability Index and Environmental Justice Index) and disparities in healthcare-acquired fungal disease incidence, including facility-level access and quality of care, and differences in clinical care by age, race, sex, and other factors.
cdc_priorities.priority_2_develop_health_equity_interve: Certain strategies can address the disproportionate burden of fungal diseases faced by some groups. Clinician education about high-risk populations can help them adapt approaches to better serve patient-specific needs. Increased access to laboratories, especially antifungal susceptibility testing, helps more people get timely appropriate treatment even in remote areas. Targeted public health education campaigns can empower higher-risk populations to take preventative actions and know when to seek care. Interventions include fungal disease outreach to high-risk populations in collaboration with the Bureau of Prisons, migrant farm worker organizations, Tribal Health Organizations, and the Indian Health Service, as well as addressing risks to migrants and refugees coming to the U.S. by raising awareness of neglected tropical diseases and studying the impact of antifungal-resistant ringworm.

health_equity.policy_note: Policy changes, education, and awareness help advance health equity, alongside data covering diverse populations to help identify health inequities.

funginet_whole_genome_sequencing.overview: FungiNet, launched in 2021, is a global community of practice — a network of laboratorians, bioinformaticians, and epidemiologists — advancing fungal pathogen genomics in public health to improve outbreak responses and surveillance.
goals: Track the spread of antimicrobial-resistant fungal pathogens.
funginet_whole_genome_sequencing.activities: Participants generate and analyze whole genome sequencing data for Candida auris (C. auris) and other fungal pathogens. Collaborators are building capacity in laboratory and bioinformatic fungal genomic analysis by developing new tools for fungal genomic analysis. FungiNet contributes genomic data to the National Center for Biotechnology Information Sequence Read Archive (NCBI SRA), a publicly accessible database.
funginet_whole_genome_sequencing.network_scope: FungiNet Domestic includes participants from across the United States, including many collaborators with the Antimicrobial Resistance Laboratory Network. FungiNet Global currently has participants in Colombia, South Africa, Spain, Bangladesh, and Argentina.
funginet_whole_genome_sequencing.how_to_participate: Public health collaborators can learn how to participate by emailing FungiNet@cdc.gov, which also provides access to the FungiNet channel on the communication application Slack.
